Ibn Qutaybah said: "He multiplies you in it," i.e., in the pair; it has been said: in the womb; it has been said: in the uterus.

﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾: the mention of the likeness here is intended to intensify the negation by way of kināyah (metonymy, an indirect expression). For when something is negated of one who is comparable to Him, its negation of Him is all the more fitting, as in the saying: "Someone like you does not stingy, and others do not generously give." It has been said that the kāf (ka, "like") is extra for emphasis, meaning "there is nothing His like," and it has been said that mithl (likeness) is extra, as said by Tha‘lab and others, as in His saying ﴿If they believe in the like of what you believed in﴾ [al-Baqarah, 137], meaning "in what you believed in." From this is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

*And slain men like the trunks of palm trees, covered by a pouring rain.*

i.e., like trunks. But the first (view) is better, for kināyah is a method used by the Arabs and a path familiar to them. From this is the saying of the poet:

*There is not like the youth Zuhayr*
*a character that matches him in virtues.*

Another said:

*For the likes of Layla a man kills himself,*
*even if he spends the night, from Layla, in despair, hungry.*

Another said:

*Sa‘d ibn Zayd, when you see their excellence,*
*there is not among people one like them.*

Ibn Qutaybah said: The Arabs put mathal (the like) in the place of the self (nafs), so they say: "One like me is not spoken to this way," meaning, "I am not spoken to this way."

Abu al-Baqa’ argued for the extra kāf, saying: if it were not extra, it would lead to an absurdity, for the meaning would be: "He has a like, and the like of His like exists," and this is contradictory, for if He had a like, then His like has a like, which is Him; and in addition, affirming a like for Allah, glorified is He, is impossible. This is a fine argument, but what he raised is answered by what we have mentioned, that the speech is meant as kināyah.

Whoever understands this noble verse as it should be understood and reflects upon it as it should be reflected upon, will proceed with it, when the disputers differ about the attributes, along a clear white path, and his insight will increase if he contemplates the meaning of His saying: ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾. For this affirmation after that negation of any like has comprised the coolness of certainty, the healing of hearts, and the calm of minds. So, O seeker of truth, appreciate the measure of this clear proof and this strong evidence, for with it you will crush many innovations, shatter the heads of misguidance, and humble the pride of groups of the overly ambitious, especially when you join to it the saying of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿And they cannot encompass Him in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha, 110]. For then you will have grasped both ends of the rope of what they call ʿilm al-kalam (scholastic theology) and ʿilm uṣūl al-dīn (the science of the principles of religion):

*Leave aside the plunder that was shouted over in its chambers,*
*and speak instead of the matter of the riding-camels.*

﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾: i.e., their treasuries, or their keys. Its verification has already been discussed in Surat al-Zumar. Maqalid is the plural of iqlīd, which means the key, and it was pluralized contrary to analogy. Al-Nahhas said: whoever owns the keys owns the treasuries.

Then, after He, glorified is He, mentioned that in His hand are the keys of the heavens and the earth, He mentioned after it extension and restriction, saying: ﴿He extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it﴾, i.e., He widens it for whom He wills of His creatures and narrows it for whom He wills. ﴿Indeed, He is, of all things, Knowing﴾: nothing is hidden from Him. The comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all things includes His knowledge of the obedience of the obedient and the disobedience of the disobedient, so He requites each according to what he deserves of good or evil.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa’i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh have related from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us with two books in his hand. He said: 'Do you know what these two books are?' We said: 'No, unless you inform us, O Messenger of Allah.' He said to the one in his right hand: 'This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, with the names of the people of Paradise, the names of their fathers and their tribes, then he summarized at its end, so nothing will be added to them and nothing will be subtracted from them.' Then he said to the one in his left: 'This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, with the names of the people of the Fire and the names of their fathers and their tribes, then he summarized at its end, so nothing will be added to them and nothing will be subtracted from them forever.' His companions said: 'Then what is the point of action, O Messenger of Allah, if the matter has already been finished?' He said: 'Be upright and draw near (to the mark), for the companion of Paradise will be sealed with the deeds of the people of Paradise, however he may act, and the companion of the Fire will be sealed with the deeds of the people of the Fire, however he may act.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gestured with his two hands, threw them away, and said: 'Your Lord has finished with the servants: ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the blaze﴾.'"

al-Tirmidhi said after relating it: "A hadith ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ gharīb (good, sound, and rare)."

Ibn Jarir related part of it from Ibn ʿAmr as a mawquf (a statement ending with a companion). Ibn Jarir said: "This mawquf version is closer to the correct."

I say: Rather, the marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet) version is closer to the correct, for it was raised by a trustworthy transmitter, and raising it is an established addition from a sound route. What strengthens the raised version is what Ibn Mardawayh related from al-Bara’, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us with a book in his hand, looking into it. They said: 'Look at him, how (can he read it) when he is unlettered and cannot read?' He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knew it, and said: 'This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, with the names of the people of Paradise and the names of their tribes, none added to them and none subtracted from them.' And he said: ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the blaze﴾. Your Lord has finished with the deeds of the servants."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 42, verses 1–12 (part 1 of 2):

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ ﴿ʿAyn Sīn﴾ [i.e., Surat al-Shura] was revealed in Makkah. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr, and al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ and Jābir likewise said.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah that it is Meccan except for four verses of it, which were revealed in Madinah: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for it any reward except affection for the near kin﴾ [al-Shura: 23–26] to its end.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Nuʿaym ibn Hammad and al-Khatib narrated from Artah ibn al-Mundhir, who said: A man came to Ibn ʿAbbas while Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yaman was with him, and said: "Tell me about the interpretation of ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ ﴿ʿAyn Sīn﴾." He turned away from him. Then he repeated his statement, and he turned away again and repeated it. Then he repeated it a third time, and he did not answer him. Ḥudhayfah said to him: "I will tell you about it. Why did he dislike it? It was revealed concerning a man from his family called ʿAbd Ilah or ʿAbd Allah, who will settle on a river of the rivers of the East, and on it he will build two cities, the river being split between them in a split. Every stubborn tyrant will gather in them. When Allah permits the end of their dominion, the cessation of their rule and their term, Allah will send a fire upon one of them by night, and in the morning it will be black, dark, burnt, as if it had never been in its place. Its companion will wake up amazed at how it was snatched away. There will be nothing but the brightness of that day until every stubborn tyrant among them gathers in it. Then Allah will sink it and them all together. That is His saying: ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ ﴿ʿAyn Sīn﴾, meaning: a determination from Allah, and a trial, and a decree of gathering, meaning: justice from Him. Sīn: meaning 'it will be'. Qāf: for these two cities."

I say: this ḥadīth is neither sound nor established, and I do not think it is anything but one of the fabricated, lying reports. What drives its fabricator to it is what happens to many people: enmity toward states, belittling them and disparaging them.

Abu Yaʿla and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated, and al-Suyuti said, with a weak chain. I say: rather, it is with a fabricated chain and a lying text, from Abu Muʿawiyah, who said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab ascended the pulpit and said: "O people, has any one of you heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explain ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ ﴿ʿAyn Sīn﴾?" Ibn ʿAbbas leapt up and said: "Ḥā Mīm is one of the names of Allah." He said: "Then ʿAyn?" He said: "ʿAyn: the one mentioned witnessed (ʿāyana) the punishment of the Day of Badr." He said: "Then Sīn?" He said: "﴿And those who have done wrong will know to what overturn they will be overturned﴾" [al-Shuʿara: 227]. He said: "Then Qāf?" and he fell silent. Abu Dharr stood up and explained it as Ibn ʿAbbas had said, and said: "Qāf is a calamity from the sky that strikes people."

Ibn Kathir said about the first ḥadīth that it is strange, wondrous and rejected (munkar), and about the second that it is stranger than the first. My own view is that both are fabricated and lying.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

As for His saying ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ ﴿ʿAyn Sīn﴾: the discussion of such opening letters (fawatih, the initial letters of surahs) has already passed. Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Fadl was asked why ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ was separated (from the following words) while ﴿Kāf Hā Yāʾ ʿAyn Ṣād﴾ was not. He said: "Because these are surahs whose first letters are Ḥā Mīm, so they follow the pattern of their counterparts. So it is as if Ḥā Mīm is the subject (mubtadaʾ, the subject of a nominal sentence) and ʿAyn Sīn its predicate (khabar, the complement of the subject). And because they (Ḥā Mīm and ʿAyn Sīn) are two verses. Their counterparts, such as Kāf Hā Yāʾ ʿAyn Ṣād, and Alif Lām Mīm, and Alif Lām Mīm Ṣād, are one verse each."

It was also said: because the people of interpretation did not differ that Kāf Hā Yāʾ ʿAyn Ṣād and its counterparts are only letters of spelling (ḥurūf al-tahajjī), but they differed about Ḥā Mīm. It was said that its meaning is ḥummа, meaning "decreed," as has already passed.

It was said: Ḥ is His forbearance (ḥilm), M His glory (majd), ʿ His knowledge (ʿilm), S His brilliance (sanāʾ), and Q His power (qudrah). Allah swore by them.

Other things have been said besides this, which are contrived and forced, for which no proof has indicated, and no argument has come, nor even the semblance of an argument. We have already mentioned before this what has been reported about it that has no basis. The truth is what we presented to you at the opening of Surat al-Baqarah.

It was said: they are two names for the surah. It was said: they are one name for it (p-1322). On the first view, they are two predicates of an elided subject (mubtadaʾ maḥdhūf); on the second, it is a predicate of that elided subject.

Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas read: "Ḥā Sīn Qāf" [not as above; reading given as "ḥam saq"].

﴿Thus He reveals to you, and to those before you, Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ This is a new statement, not connected to what precedes it, meaning: like that revelation which was revealed to the rest of the prophets from the books of Allah sent down to them, containing the call to monotheism and resurrection, is revealed to you, O Muhammad, in this surah.

It was also said: ﴿Ḥā Mīm ʿAyn Sīn﴾ was revealed to those before him among the prophets, so the reference in His saying "thus" points to it.

The majority read "yūḥī" with a kasra on the ḥāʾ, active voice, its agent being Allah. Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muḥaysin read it with a fatḥa on it, passive voice, and the substitute for the agent is a hidden pronoun referring to "thus." The sense: "Like that revelation, He reveals it to you." Or the substitute for the agent is "to you." Or it is the phrase mentioned: "this utterance is revealed to you," or "the Qur'an," or "the verbal noun of yūḥī." The noun ("Allah, the Mighty, the Wise") is raised as the agent of an elided verb, as if it were said: "Who reveals?" and it was said: "Allah, the Mighty, the Wise."

As for the reading of the majority, it is clear in both wording and meaning. A similar construction has already passed in His saying: ﴿He is glorified therein in the mornings and evenings, by men﴾ [al-Nur: 36–37]. Abu Ḥaywah, al-Aʿmash and Aban read "nūḥī" with a nūn, so ﴿Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ is in a position of accusative (naṣb), and the meaning: "We reveal to you this utterance."

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great.﴾ He, glorified be He, described Himself with this attribute, being the Owner of all that is in the heavens and the earth, because it indicates the perfection of His power and the effectiveness of His disposal over all His creatures.

﴿The heavens are almost splitting apart from above them﴾. The majority read "takādu" with the feminine ya (taʾ) and likewise "yatafaṭṭarna" (they split) read with the taʾ and a shadda on the ṭāʾ. Nafiʿ, al-Kisaʾi and Ibn Wathab read "takādu al-samāwātu yatafaṭṭarna" with the yāʾ in both. Abu ʿAmr, al-Mufaḍḍal, Abu Bakr and Abu ʿUbayd read "yatafaṭṭarna" with the yāʾ and the nūn, from infiṭār (splitting), like His saying: ﴿When the sky splits apart﴾ [al-Infitar: 1]. Tafaṭṭur means splitting open.

Al-Ḍaḥḥak and al-Suddi said: "they split open from the greatness and majesty of Allah, from above them."

It was also said: the meaning is that each of them almost splits above the one next to it, from the saying of the polytheists, "Allah has taken a son." It was also said: "from above them" means from above the earths. The first is preferable.

The "min" in ﴿min fawqihinna﴾ indicates the starting point: the splitting begins from the direction of the above.

Al-Akhfash al-Saghir said: the pronoun refers to the groups of disbelievers, meaning: "from above the groups of disbelievers." This is very far-fetched. The reason for singling out the direction of above is that it is closer to the great signs and the striking creations. Or it is by way of emphasis, as if the word of the disbelievers, though it came from the direction below, affected the direction above; so its effect in the direction below is all the more so.

﴿And the angels glorify the praise of their Lord﴾, meaning: they declare Him free of what is unfitting for Him and what is not permissible for Him, while praising Him.

It was also said: glorification (tasbīḥ) is placed in the position of wonder, meaning: they marvel at the boldness of the polytheists against Allah.

It was also said: the meaning of "with the praise of their Lord" is "by the command of their Lord," as said by al-Suddi.

﴿And they seek forgiveness for those on the earth﴾, from among the believing servants of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿And they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7]. It was also said: their seeking forgiveness means striving for what would bring forgiveness for them and postponement of their punishment, hoping for the faith of the disbeliever and the repentance of the sinner. Then the verse is general, as is the apparent wording, not specific to the believers, even though they are included in it in the first degree.

﴿Unquestionably, Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾, meaning: abundant in forgiveness and mercy toward the people of His obedience and His allies, or toward all His servants, for the postponement of the punishment of the disbelievers and the disobedient is a kind of His forgiveness and mercy.

﴿As for those who take protectors other than Him﴾, meaning: idols they worship, ﴿Allah is Watchful over them﴾, meaning: He preserves their deeds in order to repay them for them. ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾, meaning: He has not appointed you over them so that you would be held to account for their sins, nor has their guidance been entrusted to you; upon you is only the delivery (of the message). It was said: this verse is abrogated (mansukhah, annulled) by the verse of the sword.

﴿And thus We revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an﴾, meaning: like that revelation, We revealed to you. "Qur'anan" is the object (mafʿūl) of "awḥaynā," and the meaning: "We sent down to you an Arabic Qur'an in the language of your people, just as We sent every messenger in the language of his people."

﴿That you may warn the Mother of Cities﴾, which is Makkah, and what is meant is its people and the people around it. The second object is elided, meaning: that you may warn them of the punishment.

﴿And warn of the Day of Gathering﴾, meaning: and that you may warn about the Day of Gathering, which is the Day of Resurrection, because it is the gathering place of all creation.

It was also said: what is meant is the gathering of souls with bodies. It was said: the gathering of the wrongdoer and the wronged. It was said: the gathering of the doer and the deed.

﴿About which there is no doubt﴾, meaning: there is no uncertainty about it. The sentence is parenthetical, confirming what precedes it, or it is a description of the Day of Gathering, or a circumstance from it.

﴿A party will be in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾. The majority read "farīqun" in both places with a ḍamma (nominative), either as a subject with the prepositional phrase as its predicate, and it is permissible to begin with an indefinite noun because the context is one of detailing; or the predicate is elided before it, meaning: "among them is a party in Paradise and among them a party in the Blaze"; or it is the predicate of an elided subject, a pronoun referring to the two groups implied by mention of the gathering, meaning: "they are a party in Paradise and a party in the Blaze."

Zayd ibn ʿAli read "farīqan" with a fatḥa (accusative) in both places as a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause from an elided sentence, meaning: "they separated while being in that state." Al-Farrāʾ and al-Kisaʾi permitted the accusative on the basis of an assumed "so that you warn a party."

﴿Had Allah willed, He would have made them one community﴾. Al-Ḍaḥḥak said: "the people of one religion, either upon guidance or upon misguidance. But they separated into differing religions by eternal will." This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿But He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾, into the true religion, which is Islam. ﴿And the wrongdoers have no protector or helper﴾, meaning: the polytheists have no protector who repels punishment from them, nor a helper who supports them in that position. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 35], and His saying: ﴿Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ [al-Sajdah: 13]. There are disputes here among the partisans of schools, defending what their predecessors had followed and what those after them trod upon. For us, there is no benefit in mentioning any of that, as is our custom in this tafsir. It is a Salafi tafsir that moves with the truth and turns with the implications of the noble text, and only one whose foot is firmly planted, and whose heart, flesh and blood are free of partisanship, can recognise this (p-1323).

The sentence ﴿Or have they taken protectors other than Him?﴾ is a new statement confirming what precedes it, namely that the wrongdoers have no protector or helper. This "am" is the disjunctive one, implying the meaning of "bal" (rather), which indicates transition, and the interrogative hamza, which indicates denial. The meaning: "Rather, have the disbelievers taken protectors other than Allah, from among the idols they worship?"

﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾, meaning: He is the one worthy of being taken as a protector, for He is the Creator, the Provider, the One who harms and benefits. It was also said: the fāʾ is the answer to an elided condition, meaning: "If they intend to take a protector in truth, then Allah is the Protector." ﴿He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things Competent﴾, meaning: He has power over everything possible, so He is the one worthy of being singled out for divinity and of being singled out for worship.

﴿Whatever you differ over, its ruling is with Allah﴾. This is general for everything over which the servants differ concerning matters of religion. Its judgement and its reference are to Allah, who judges concerning it on the Day of Resurrection with His ruling, and decides the dispute of the disputants about it. At that point the true is distinguished from the false, and the party of Paradise and the party of the Fire are separated.

Al-Kalbi said: "Whatever you differ over, of anything, meaning in the matter of religion, its ruling is with Allah, who decides concerning it."

Muqatil said: "The people of Makkah, some of them disbelieved in the Qur'an and some believed in it, so this was revealed." The lesson is in the generality of the wording, not in the specificity of the occasion of revelation.

It may be said that the meaning of "His judgment is with Allah" is that it is referred back to His Book, for it encompasses judgment among His servants concerning what they dispute. So the verse is general: every dispute concerning matters of religion is referred back to the Book of Allah. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa’, 59]. He, glorified is He, has ruled that the religion is Islam, that the Qur'an is true, and that the believers are in Paradise while the disbelievers are in the Fire. But since the disbelievers do not submit to this being true except in the Hereafter, Allah promised them this on the Day of Resurrection. That is the Judge who rules by this judgment. ﴿That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I have relied﴾: I depended upon Him in all my affairs, not on anyone else, and I entrusted Him with all my concerns. ﴿And to Him I turn in repentance﴾: i.e., I return to Him in everything that confronts me, not to anyone else.

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾: al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read it in the nominative, either as another predicate of ﴿dhalikum﴾, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a subject whose predicate is what follows, or as an adjective of rabbi, since the idafah (genitive construction) is maḥḍah (pure, i.e., definite). In this last case, ﴿upon Him I have relied and to Him I turn﴾ comes as a parenthetical between the adjective and the noun it modifies.

Zayd ibn ʿAli read فاطِرِ (fāṭiri) with a genitive case ending (jarr), making it an adjective of the noble name in the phrase ﴿to Allah﴾, with what comes between them being a parenthetical or a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in عَلَيْهِ (ʿalayhi) or إلَيْهِ (ilayhi). Al-Kisa'i permitted the accusative (naṣb) by way of address (nidāʾ), and others permitted it by way of praise (madḥ). Al-fāṭir means the creator, the originator, and its verification has already been discussed.

﴿He made for you spouses from among yourselves﴾: i.e., He created for you, from your own kind, wives. Or the intended meaning is Hawwa’ (Eve), because she was created from Adam's rib.

Mujahid said: "offspring after offspring." ﴿And of the livestock, pairs﴾: i.e., He created for the livestock, from their own kind, females; or He created for you from the livestock kinds of males and females, and these are the eight mentioned in al-An‘am. ﴿He multiplies you thereby﴾: i.e., He scatters you through it, from dhar’ (scattering), which means dispersal; or He creates you and brings you into being. The pronoun in يَذْرَؤُكم (yadhra'ukum) refers to the addressees and to the livestock, but the rational beings have precedence in it. The pronoun in فِيهِ (fihi) refers to the making (jaʿl) implied by the verb, and it has been said that it refers to the arrangement mentioned.

Al-Farra’, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning of يَذْرَؤُكم فِيهِ (yadhra'ukum fihi) is "He multiplies you by it," i.e., He multiplies you by making you into pairs, because that is the cause of offspring. Ibn Qutaybah said: "He multiplies you in it," i.e., in the pair; it has been said: in the womb; it has been said: in the uterus.

﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾: the mention of the likeness here is intended to intensify the negation by way of kināyah (metonymy, an indirect expression). For when something is negated of one who is comparable to Him, its negation of Him is all the more fitting, as in the saying: "Someone like you does not stingy, and others do not generously give." It has been said that the kāf (ka, "like") is extra for emphasis, meaning "there is nothing His like," and it has been said that mithl (likeness) is extra, as said by Tha‘lab and others, as in His saying ﴿If they believe in the like of what you believed in﴾ [al-Baqarah, 137], meaning "in what you believed in." From this is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

*And slain men like the trunks of palm trees, covered by a pouring rain.*

i.e., like trunks. But the first (view) is better, for kināyah is a method used by the Arabs and a path familiar to them. From this is the saying of the poet:

*There is not like the youth Zuhayr*
*a character that matches him in virtues.*

Another said:

*For the likes of Layla a man kills himself,*
*even if he spends the night, from Layla, in despair, hungry.*

Another said:

*Sa‘d ibn Zayd, when you see their excellence,*
*there is not among people one like them.*

Ibn Qutaybah said: The Arabs put mathal (the like) in the place of the self (nafs), so they say: "One like me is not spoken to this way," meaning, "I am not spoken to this way."

Abu al-Baqa’ argued for the extra kāf, saying: if it were not extra, it would lead to an absurdity, for the meaning would be: "He has a like, and the like of His like exists," and this is contradictory, for if He had a like, then His like has a like, which is Him; and in addition, affirming a like for Allah, glorified is He, is impossible. This is a fine argument, but what he raised is answered by what we have mentioned, that the speech is meant as kināyah.

Whoever understands this noble verse as it should be understood and reflects upon it as it should be reflected upon, will proceed with it, when the disputers differ about the attributes, along a clear white path, and his insight will increase if he contemplates the meaning of His saying: ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾. For this affirmation after that negation of any like has comprised the coolness of certainty, the healing of hearts, and the calm of minds. So, O seeker of truth, appreciate the measure of this clear proof and this strong evidence, for with it you will crush many innovations, shatter the heads of misguidance, and humble the pride of groups of the overly ambitious, especially when you join to it the saying of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿And they cannot encompass Him in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha, 110]. For then you will have grasped both ends of the rope of what they call ʿilm al-kalam (scholastic theology) and ʿilm uṣūl al-dīn (the science of the principles of religion):

*Leave aside the plunder that was shouted over in its chambers,*
*and speak instead of the matter of the riding-camels.*

﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾: i.e., their treasuries, or their keys. Its verification has already been discussed in Surat al-Zumar. Maqalid is the plural of iqlīd, which means the key, and it was pluralized contrary to analogy. Al-Nahhas said: whoever owns the keys owns the treasuries.

Then, after He, glorified is He, mentioned that in His hand are the keys of the heavens and the earth, He mentioned after it extension and restriction, saying: ﴿He extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it﴾, i.e., He widens it for whom He wills of His creatures and narrows it for whom He wills. ﴿Indeed, He is, of all things, Knowing﴾: nothing is hidden from Him. The comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all things includes His knowledge of the obedience of the obedient and the disobedience of the disobedient, so He requites each according to what he deserves of good or evil.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa’i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh have related from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us with two books in his hand. He said: 'Do you know what these two books are?' We said: 'No, unless you inform us, O Messenger of Allah.' He said to the one in his right hand: 'This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, with the names of the people of Paradise, the names of their fathers and their tribes, then he summarized at its end, so nothing will be added to them and nothing will be subtracted from them.' Then he said to the one in his left: 'This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, with the names of the people of the Fire and the names of their fathers and their tribes, then he summarized at its end, so nothing will be added to them and nothing will be subtracted from them forever.' His companions said: 'Then what is the point of action, O Messenger of Allah, if the matter has already been finished?' He said: 'Be upright and draw near (to the mark), for the companion of Paradise will be sealed with the deeds of the people of Paradise, however he may act, and the companion of the Fire will be sealed with the deeds of the people of the Fire, however he may act.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gestured with his two hands, threw them away, and said: 'Your Lord has finished with the servants: ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the blaze﴾.'"

al-Tirmidhi said after relating it: "A hadith ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ gharīb (good, sound, and rare)."

Ibn Jarir related part of it from Ibn ʿAmr as a mawquf (a statement ending with a companion). Ibn Jarir said: "This mawquf version is closer to the correct."

I say: Rather, the marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet) version is closer to the correct, for it was raised by a trustworthy transmitter, and raising it is an established addition from a sound route. What strengthens the raised version is what Ibn Mardawayh related from al-Bara’, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us with a book in his hand, looking into it. They said: 'Look at him, how (can he read it) when he is unlettered and cannot read?' He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knew it, and said: 'This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, with the names of the people of Paradise and the names of their tribes, none added to them and none subtracted from them.' And he said: ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the blaze﴾. Your Lord has finished with the deeds of the servants."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 42, verses 1–12 (part 1 of 2):

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ ﴿ʿAyn Sīn﴾ [i.e., Surat al-Shura] was revealed in Makkah. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr, and al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ and Jābir likewise said.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah that it is Meccan except for four verses of it, which were revealed in Madinah: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for it any reward except affection for the near kin﴾ [al-Shura: 23–26] to its end.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Nuʿaym ibn Hammad and al-Khatib narrated from Artah ibn al-Mundhir, who said: A man came to Ibn ʿAbbas while Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yaman was with him, and said: "Tell me about the interpretation of ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ ﴿ʿAyn Sīn﴾." He turned away from him. Then he repeated his statement, and he turned away again and repeated it. Then he repeated it a third time, and he did not answer him. Ḥudhayfah said to him: "I will tell you about it. Why did he dislike it? It was revealed concerning a man from his family called ʿAbd Ilah or ʿAbd Allah, who will settle on a river of the rivers of the East, and on it he will build two cities, the river being split between them in a split. Every stubborn tyrant will gather in them. When Allah permits the end of their dominion, the cessation of their rule and their term, Allah will send a fire upon one of them by night, and in the morning it will be black, dark, burnt, as if it had never been in its place. Its companion will wake up amazed at how it was snatched away. There will be nothing but the brightness of that day until every stubborn tyrant among them gathers in it. Then Allah will sink it and them all together. That is His saying: ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ ﴿ʿAyn Sīn﴾, meaning: a determination from Allah, and a trial, and a decree of gathering, meaning: justice from Him. Sīn: meaning 'it will be'. Qāf: for these two cities."

I say: this ḥadīth is neither sound nor established, and I do not think it is anything but one of the fabricated, lying reports. What drives its fabricator to it is what happens to many people: enmity toward states, belittling them and disparaging them.

Abu Yaʿla and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated, and al-Suyuti said, with a weak chain. I say: rather, it is with a fabricated chain and a lying text, from Abu Muʿawiyah, who said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab ascended the pulpit and said: "O people, has any one of you heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explain ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ ﴿ʿAyn Sīn﴾?" Ibn ʿAbbas leapt up and said: "Ḥā Mīm is one of the names of Allah." He said: "Then ʿAyn?" He said: "ʿAyn: the one mentioned witnessed (ʿāyana) the punishment of the Day of Badr." He said: "Then Sīn?" He said: "﴿And those who have done wrong will know to what overturn they will be overturned﴾" [al-Shuʿara: 227]. He said: "Then Qāf?" and he fell silent. Abu Dharr stood up and explained it as Ibn ʿAbbas had said, and said: "Qāf is a calamity from the sky that strikes people."

Ibn Kathir said about the first ḥadīth that it is strange, wondrous and rejected (munkar), and about the second that it is stranger than the first. My own view is that both are fabricated and lying.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

As for His saying ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ ﴿ʿAyn Sīn﴾: the discussion of such opening letters (fawatih, the initial letters of surahs) has already passed. Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Fadl was asked why ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ was separated (from the following words) while ﴿Kāf Hā Yāʾ ʿAyn Ṣād﴾ was not. He said: "Because these are surahs whose first letters are Ḥā Mīm, so they follow the pattern of their counterparts. So it is as if Ḥā Mīm is the subject (mubtadaʾ, the subject of a nominal sentence) and ʿAyn Sīn its predicate (khabar, the complement of the subject). And because they (Ḥā Mīm and ʿAyn Sīn) are two verses. Their counterparts, such as Kāf Hā Yāʾ ʿAyn Ṣād, and Alif Lām Mīm, and Alif Lām Mīm Ṣād, are one verse each."

It was also said: because the people of interpretation did not differ that Kāf Hā Yāʾ ʿAyn Ṣād and its counterparts are only letters of spelling (ḥurūf al-tahajjī), but they differed about Ḥā Mīm. It was said that its meaning is ḥummа, meaning "decreed," as has already passed.

It was said: Ḥ is His forbearance (ḥilm), M His glory (majd), ʿ His knowledge (ʿilm), S His brilliance (sanāʾ), and Q His power (qudrah). Allah swore by them.

Other things have been said besides this, which are contrived and forced, for which no proof has indicated, and no argument has come, nor even the semblance of an argument. We have already mentioned before this what has been reported about it that has no basis. The truth is what we presented to you at the opening of Surat al-Baqarah.

It was said: they are two names for the surah. It was said: they are one name for it (p-1322). On the first view, they are two predicates of an elided subject (mubtadaʾ maḥdhūf); on the second, it is a predicate of that elided subject.

Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas read: "Ḥā Sīn Qāf" [not as above; reading given as "ḥam saq"].

﴿Thus He reveals to you, and to those before you, Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ This is a new statement, not connected to what precedes it, meaning: like that revelation which was revealed to the rest of the prophets from the books of Allah sent down to them, containing the call to monotheism and resurrection, is revealed to you, O Muhammad, in this surah.

It was also said: ﴿Ḥā Mīm ʿAyn Sīn﴾ was revealed to those before him among the prophets, so the reference in His saying "thus" points to it.

The majority read "yūḥī" with a kasra on the ḥāʾ, active voice, its agent being Allah. Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muḥaysin read it with a fatḥa on it, passive voice, and the substitute for the agent is a hidden pronoun referring to "thus." The sense: "Like that revelation, He reveals it to you." Or the substitute for the agent is "to you." Or it is the phrase mentioned: "this utterance is revealed to you," or "the Qur'an," or "the verbal noun of yūḥī." The noun ("Allah, the Mighty, the Wise") is raised as the agent of an elided verb, as if it were said: "Who reveals?" and it was said: "Allah, the Mighty, the Wise."

As for the reading of the majority, it is clear in both wording and meaning. A similar construction has already passed in His saying: ﴿He is glorified therein in the mornings and evenings, by men﴾ [al-Nur: 36–37]. Abu Ḥaywah, al-Aʿmash and Aban read "nūḥī" with a nūn, so ﴿Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ is in a position of accusative (naṣb), and the meaning: "We reveal to you this utterance."

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great.﴾ He, glorified be He, described Himself with this attribute, being the Owner of all that is in the heavens and the earth, because it indicates the perfection of His power and the effectiveness of His disposal over all His creatures.

﴿The heavens are almost splitting apart from above them﴾. The majority read "takādu" with the feminine ya (taʾ) and likewise "yatafaṭṭarna" (they split) read with the taʾ and a shadda on the ṭāʾ. Nafiʿ, al-Kisaʾi and Ibn Wathab read "takādu al-samāwātu yatafaṭṭarna" with the yāʾ in both. Abu ʿAmr, al-Mufaḍḍal, Abu Bakr and Abu ʿUbayd read "yatafaṭṭarna" with the yāʾ and the nūn, from infiṭār (splitting), like His saying: ﴿When the sky splits apart﴾ [al-Infitar: 1]. Tafaṭṭur means splitting open.

Al-Ḍaḥḥak and al-Suddi said: "they split open from the greatness and majesty of Allah, from above them."

It was also said: the meaning is that each of them almost splits above the one next to it, from the saying of the polytheists, "Allah has taken a son." It was also said: "from above them" means from above the earths. The first is preferable.

The "min" in ﴿min fawqihinna﴾ indicates the starting point: the splitting begins from the direction of the above.

Al-Akhfash al-Saghir said: the pronoun refers to the groups of disbelievers, meaning: "from above the groups of disbelievers." This is very far-fetched. The reason for singling out the direction of above is that it is closer to the great signs and the striking creations. Or it is by way of emphasis, as if the word of the disbelievers, though it came from the direction below, affected the direction above; so its effect in the direction below is all the more so.

﴿And the angels glorify the praise of their Lord﴾, meaning: they declare Him free of what is unfitting for Him and what is not permissible for Him, while praising Him.

It was also said: glorification (tasbīḥ) is placed in the position of wonder, meaning: they marvel at the boldness of the polytheists against Allah.

It was also said: the meaning of "with the praise of their Lord" is "by the command of their Lord," as said by al-Suddi.

﴿And they seek forgiveness for those on the earth﴾, from among the believing servants of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿And they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7]. It was also said: their seeking forgiveness means striving for what would bring forgiveness for them and postponement of their punishment, hoping for the faith of the disbeliever and the repentance of the sinner. Then the verse is general, as is the apparent wording, not specific to the believers, even though they are included in it in the first degree.

﴿Unquestionably, Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾, meaning: abundant in forgiveness and mercy toward the people of His obedience and His allies, or toward all His servants, for the postponement of the punishment of the disbelievers and the disobedient is a kind of His forgiveness and mercy.

﴿As for those who take protectors other than Him﴾, meaning: idols they worship, ﴿Allah is Watchful over them﴾, meaning: He preserves their deeds in order to repay them for them. ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾, meaning: He has not appointed you over them so that you would be held to account for their sins, nor has their guidance been entrusted to you; upon you is only the delivery (of the message). It was said: this verse is abrogated (mansukhah, annulled) by the verse of the sword.

﴿And thus We revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an﴾, meaning: like that revelation, We revealed to you. "Qur'anan" is the object (mafʿūl) of "awḥaynā," and the meaning: "We sent down to you an Arabic Qur'an in the language of your people, just as We sent every messenger in the language of his people."

﴿That you may warn the Mother of Cities﴾, which is Makkah, and what is meant is its people and the people around it. The second object is elided, meaning: that you may warn them of the punishment.

﴿And warn of the Day of Gathering﴾, meaning: and that you may warn about the Day of Gathering, which is the Day of Resurrection, because it is the gathering place of all creation.

It was also said: what is meant is the gathering of souls with bodies. It was said: the gathering of the wrongdoer and the wronged. It was said: the gathering of the doer and the deed.

﴿About which there is no doubt﴾, meaning: there is no uncertainty about it. The sentence is parenthetical, confirming what precedes it, or it is a description of the Day of Gathering, or a circumstance from it.

﴿A party will be in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾. The majority read "farīqun" in both places with a ḍamma (nominative), either as a subject with the prepositional phrase as its predicate, and it is permissible to begin with an indefinite noun because the context is one of detailing; or the predicate is elided before it, meaning: "among them is a party in Paradise and among them a party in the Blaze"; or it is the predicate of an elided subject, a pronoun referring to the two groups implied by mention of the gathering, meaning: "they are a party in Paradise and a party in the Blaze."

Zayd ibn ʿAli read "farīqan" with a fatḥa (accusative) in both places as a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause from an elided sentence, meaning: "they separated while being in that state." Al-Farrāʾ and al-Kisaʾi permitted the accusative on the basis of an assumed "so that you warn a party."

﴿Had Allah willed, He would have made them one community﴾. Al-Ḍaḥḥak said: "the people of one religion, either upon guidance or upon misguidance. But they separated into differing religions by eternal will." This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿But He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾, into the true religion, which is Islam. ﴿And the wrongdoers have no protector or helper﴾, meaning: the polytheists have no protector who repels punishment from them, nor a helper who supports them in that position. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 35], and His saying: ﴿Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ [al-Sajdah: 13]. There are disputes here among the partisans of schools, defending what their predecessors had followed and what those after them trod upon. For us, there is no benefit in mentioning any of that, as is our custom in this tafsir. It is a Salafi tafsir that moves with the truth and turns with the implications of the noble text, and only one whose foot is firmly planted, and whose heart, flesh and blood are free of partisanship, can recognise this (p-1323).

The sentence ﴿Or have they taken protectors other than Him?﴾ is a new statement confirming what precedes it, namely that the wrongdoers have no protector or helper. This "am" is the disjunctive one, implying the meaning of "bal" (rather), which indicates transition, and the interrogative hamza, which indicates denial. The meaning: "Rather, have the disbelievers taken protectors other than Allah, from among the idols they worship?"

﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾, meaning: He is the one worthy of being taken as a protector, for He is the Creator, the Provider, the One who harms and benefits. It was also said: the fāʾ is the answer to an elided condition, meaning: "If they intend to take a protector in truth, then Allah is the Protector." ﴿He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things Competent﴾, meaning: He has power over everything possible, so He is the one worthy of being singled out for divinity and of being singled out for worship.

﴿Whatever you differ over, its ruling is with Allah﴾. This is general for everything over which the servants differ concerning matters of religion. Its judgement and its reference are to Allah, who judges concerning it on the Day of Resurrection with His ruling, and decides the dispute of the disputants about it. At that point the true is distinguished from the false, and the party of Paradise and the party of the Fire are separated.

Al-Kalbi said: "Whatever you differ over, of anything, meaning in the matter of religion, its ruling is with Allah, who decides concerning it."

Muqatil said: "The people of Makkah, some of them disbelieved in the Qur'an and some believed in it, so this was revealed." The lesson is in the generality of the wording, not in the specificity of the occasion of revelation.

It may be said that the meaning of "His judgment is with Allah" is that it is referred back to His Book, for it encompasses judgment among His servants concerning what they dispute. So the verse is general: every dispute concerning matters of religion is referred back to the Book of Allah. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa’, 59]. He, glorified is He, has ruled that the religion is Islam, that the Qur'an is true, and that the believers are in Paradise while the disbelievers are in the Fire. But since the disbelievers do not submit to this being true except in the Hereafter, Allah promised them this on the Day of Resurrection. That is the Judge who rules by this judgment. ﴿That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I have relied﴾: I depended upon Him in all my affairs, not on anyone else, and I entrusted Him with all my concerns. ﴿And to Him I turn in repentance﴾: i.e., I return to Him in everything that confronts me, not to anyone else.

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾: al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read it in the nominative, either as another predicate of ﴿dhalikum﴾, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a subject whose predicate is what follows, or as an adjective of rabbi, since the idafah (genitive construction) is maḥḍah (pure, i.e., definite). In this last case, ﴿upon Him I have relied and to Him I turn﴾ comes as a parenthetical between the adjective and the noun it modifies.

Zayd ibn ʿAli read فاطِرِ (fāṭiri) with a genitive case ending (jarr), making it an adjective of the noble name in the phrase ﴿to Allah﴾, with what comes between them being a parenthetical or a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in عَلَيْهِ (ʿalayhi) or إلَيْهِ (ilayhi). Al-Kisa'i permitted the accusative (naṣb) by way of address (nidāʾ), and others permitted it by way of praise (madḥ). Al-fāṭir means the creator, the originator, and its verification has already been discussed.

﴿He made for you spouses from among yourselves﴾: i.e., He created for you, from your own kind, wives. Or the intended meaning is Hawwa’ (Eve), because she was created from Adam's rib.

Mujahid said: "offspring after offspring." ﴿And of the livestock, pairs﴾: i.e., He created for the livestock, from their own kind, females; or He created for you from the livestock kinds of males and females, and these are the eight mentioned in al-An‘am. ﴿He multiplies you thereby﴾: i.e., He scatters you through it, from dhar’ (scattering), which means dispersal; or He creates you and brings you into being. The pronoun in يَذْرَؤُكم (yadhra'ukum) refers to the addressees and to the livestock, but the rational beings have precedence in it. The pronoun in فِيهِ (fihi) refers to the making (jaʿl) implied by the verb, and it has been said that it refers to the arrangement mentioned.

Al-Farra’, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning of يَذْرَؤُكم فِيهِ (yadhra'ukum fihi) is "He multiplies you by it," i.e., He multiplies you by making you into pairs, because that is the cause of offspring. Ibn Qutaybah said: "He multiplies you in it," i.e., in the pair; it has been said: in the womb; it has been said: in the uterus.

﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾: the mention of the likeness here is intended to intensify the negation by way of kināyah (metonymy, an indirect expression). For when something is negated of one who is comparable to Him, its negation of Him is all the more fitting, as in the saying: "Someone like you does not stingy, and others do not generously give." It has been said that the kāf (ka, "like") is extra for emphasis, meaning "there is nothing His like," and it has been said that mithl (likeness) is extra, as said by Tha‘lab and others, as in His saying ﴿If they believe in the like of what you believed in﴾ [al-Baqarah, 137], meaning "in what you believed in." From this is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

*And slain men like the trunks of palm trees, covered by a pouring rain.*

i.e., like trunks. But the first (view) is better, for kināyah is a method used by the Arabs and a path familiar to them. From this is the saying of the poet:

*There is not like the youth Zuhayr*
*a character that matches him in virtues.*

Another said:

*For the likes of Layla a man kills himself,*
*even if he spends the night, from Layla, in despair, hungry.*

Another said:

*Sa‘d ibn Zayd, when you see their excellence,*
*there is not among people one like them.*

Ibn Qutaybah said: The Arabs put mathal (the like) in the place of the self (nafs), so they say: "One like me is not spoken to this way," meaning, "I am not spoken to this way."

Abu al-Baqa’ argued for the extra kāf, saying: if it were not extra, it would lead to an absurdity, for the meaning would be: "He has a like, and the like of His like exists," and this is contradictory, for if He had a like, then His like has a like, which is Him; and in addition, affirming a like for Allah, glorified is He, is impossible. This is a fine argument, but what he raised is answered by what we have mentioned, that the speech is meant as kināyah.

Whoever understands this noble verse as it should be understood and reflects upon it as it should be reflected upon, will proceed with it, when the disputers differ about the attributes, along a clear white path, and his insight will increase if he contemplates the meaning of His saying: ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾. For this affirmation after that negation of any like has comprised the coolness of certainty, the healing of hearts, and the calm of minds. So, O seeker of truth, appreciate the measure of this clear proof and this strong evidence, for with it you will crush many innovations, shatter the heads of misguidance, and humble the pride of groups of the overly ambitious, especially when you join to it the saying of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿And they cannot encompass Him in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha, 110]. For then you will have grasped both ends of the rope of what they call ʿilm al-kalam (scholastic theology) and ʿilm uṣūl al-dīn (the science of the principles of religion):

*Leave aside the plunder that was shouted over in its chambers,*
*and speak instead of the matter of the riding-camels.*

﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾: i.e., their treasuries, or their keys. Its verification has already been discussed in Surat al-Zumar. Maqalid is the plural of iqlīd, which means the key, and it was pluralized contrary to analogy. Al-Nahhas said: whoever owns the keys owns the treasuries.

Then, after He, glorified is He, mentioned that in His hand are the keys of the heavens and the earth, He mentioned after it extension and restriction, saying: ﴿He extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it﴾, i.e., He widens it for whom He wills of His creatures and narrows it for whom He wills. ﴿Indeed, He is, of all things, Knowing﴾: nothing is hidden from Him. The comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all things includes His knowledge of the obedience of the obedient and the disobedience of the disobedient, so He requites each according to what he deserves of good or evil.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa’i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh have related from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us with two books in his hand. He said: 'Do you know what these two books are?' We said: 'No, unless you inform us, O Messenger of Allah.' He said to the one in his right hand: 'This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, with the names of the people of Paradise, the names of their fathers and their tribes, then he summarized at its end, so nothing will be added to them and nothing will be subtracted from them.' Then he said to the one in his left: 'This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, with the names of the people of the Fire and the names of their fathers and their tribes, then he summarized at its end, so nothing will be added to them and nothing will be subtracted from them forever.' His companions said: 'Then what is the point of action, O Messenger of Allah, if the matter has already been finished?' He said: 'Be upright and draw near (to the mark), for the companion of Paradise will be sealed with the deeds of the people of Paradise, however he may act, and the companion of the Fire will be sealed with the deeds of the people of the Fire, however he may act.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gestured with his two hands, threw them away, and said: 'Your Lord has finished with the servants: ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the blaze﴾.'"

al-Tirmidhi said after relating it: "A hadith ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ gharīb (good, sound, and rare)."

Ibn Jarir related part of it from Ibn ʿAmr as a mawquf (a statement ending with a companion). Ibn Jarir said: "This mawquf version is closer to the correct."

I say: Rather, the marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet) version is closer to the correct, for it was raised by a trustworthy transmitter, and raising it is an established addition from a sound route. What strengthens the raised version is what Ibn Mardawayh related from al-Bara’, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us with a book in his hand, looking into it. They said: 'Look at him, how (can he read it) when he is unlettered and cannot read?' He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knew it, and said: 'This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, with the names of the people of Paradise and the names of their tribes, none added to them and none subtracted from them.' And he said: ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the blaze﴾. Your Lord has finished with the deeds of the servants."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 42, verses 13–18 (part 1 of 2):

The address in His words ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion﴾ is to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). That is, He has clarified and made clear for you of the religion ﴿that which He enjoined upon Noah﴾, namely the Tawhid (Oneness of God), the religion of Islam, and the fundamental principles of the sacred laws (shara'i') in which the Messengers did not differ and upon which the Books agreed; ﴿and that which We revealed to you﴾, namely the Qur'an, the laws of Islam, and disavowal of polytheism. The expression of it by the relative pronoun is to magnify its status. He specified what He prescribed for our Prophet (ﷺ) with the revelation, although what comes before and after it is mentioned with the injunction, to make explicit his Messengership. ﴿And that which We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses and Jesus﴾, of what the laws agree upon.

Then He explained what those [prophets] were enjoined, saying: ﴿that you establish the religion﴾, that is, the Oneness of God, faith in Him, obedience to His Messengers, and acceptance of their laws. "An" (that) here is the verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle, and it and what follows it are in the nominative position as a predicate of an omitted subject, as if it were said: "What is that which God prescribed?" It was said: "It is the establishment of the religion." Or it is in the accusative position as a substitute for the relative pronoun, or in the genitive position as a substitute for "the religion," or it is the explanatory (mufassirah) "an," since a meaning of saying has preceded it. Muqatil said: he means that He prescribed for you and for those before you among the Prophets one religion. Muqatil said: he means the Tawhid. Mujahid said: God never sent a Prophet except that He enjoined upon him the establishment of prayer, the giving of zakat, and acknowledgment of obedience to God; that is His religion which He prescribed for them.

Qatadah said: he means the making lawful of the lawful and the making unlawful of the unlawful. Abraham, Moses and Jesus were singled out for mention along with our Prophet (ﷺ) because they are the possessors of sacred laws.

Then, when He commanded them to establish the religion, He forbade them to differ concerning it, saying: ﴿and do not be divided therein﴾, that is, do not differ regarding the Tawhid, faith in God, obedience to His Messengers, and acceptance of their laws, for these matters are those upon which the sacred laws agree and the religions concur, so disagreement regarding such things is not fitting. Not of this are the subsidiary matters (furu' al-masa'il) in which the evidences differ, the indications conflict, and the understandings vary, for these are the arenas of ijtihad (independent reasoning) and the places of legitimate disagreement.

Then He mentioned that what He prescribed of the religion was burdensome to the polytheists, saying: ﴿Burdensome to the polytheists is that to which you call them﴾, that is, what you call them to of Tawhid and rejection of idols was great and difficult for them.

Qatadah said: "It was burdensome to the polytheists and grievous to them, the testimony that there is no god but God alone, and Iblis and his hosts were distressed by it, but God refused except that He would support it, exalt it, make it manifest, and grant it victory over those who oppose it."

Then He singled out His friends, saying: ﴿God chooses for Himself whom He wills﴾, that is, He selects; ijtiba' (choosing) is selection, and the meaning is: He selects for His Tawhid and entry into His religion whomever He wills of His servants. ﴿And guides to Himself whoever turns back﴾, that is, He grants success to His religion and sincerely dedicates to His worship whoever returns to His obedience and turns to His worship.

Then, when He mentioned what He prescribed for them of establishing the religion and not being divided in it, He mentioned what occurred of division and disagreement, saying: ﴿And they did not become divided except after knowledge had come to them﴾, that is, they did not divide except knowingly that division is misguidance; so they did that division out of transgression among themselves, through seeking leadership and intense partisanship. It was said: the intended are the Quraysh, who divided after knowledge had come to them, that is Muhammad (ﷺ), out of transgression against him. They used to say what God related of them in His words: ﴿And they swore by God their most emphatic oaths that if a warner came to them…﴾ [Fatir: 42], and in His words: ﴿But when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]. Then He singled out His friends, saying: ﴿God chooses for Himself whom He wills﴾, that is, He selects; ijtiba' (choosing) is selection, and the meaning is: He selects for His Tawhid and entry into His religion whomever He wills of His servants. ﴿And guides to Himself whoever turns back﴾, that is, He grants success to His religion and sincerely dedicates to His worship whoever returns to His obedience and turns to His worship.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And those who argue about Allah after He has been responded to﴾, that he said: They are the People of the Book, who used to dispute with the Muslims and turn them away from guidance, after they had responded to Allah.

And he said: They are a people of misguidance, who used to wait for the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) to come to them.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And those who argue about Allah﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: They are the Jews and the Christians. ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated a similar report from al-Hasan.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿIkrimah, who said: When ﴿When the help of Allah comes, and the victory﴾ [al-Nasr: 1] was revealed, the polytheists said to those among them who were Muslims: "People have entered the religion of Allah in multitudes, so leave from among us." Then ﴿And those who argue about Allah﴾ to the end of the verse was revealed.

The Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 42, verses 19–28 (part 1 of 2):

His words, ﴿Allah is Subtly Kind (latif) to His servants﴾: that is, He is greatly kind to them and extremely compassionate toward them.

Muqatil said: "Latif toward the righteous and the wicked, in that He does not kill them with hunger because of their sins." Ikrimah said: "Bārr (kind) toward them." Al-Suddi said: "Rafiq (gentle) toward them." It was also said: "Ḥafiyy (solicitous) toward them." Al-Qurtubi said: "Latif toward them in the presentation (of deeds) and in the reckoning," and other things have been said.

The meaning is that He extends His kindness to His servants in all their affairs, and among that is the provision (rizq) by which they live in this world. This is the meaning of His words, ﴿He provides for whom He wills﴾ from among them, however He wills. So He widens it for one and restricts it for another. ﴿And He is the Strong﴾, the Mighty in power, the Overpowering, the Capable, the Dominant who overcomes everything and is not overcome by anything.

﴿Whoever desires the tilth (ḥarth) of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his tilth﴾. Ḥarth in the language means earning. It is said: "He tills (yaḥruthu) for his dependants," and "yaḥtarith," meaning he earns. From this, a man is named Ḥārith. The original meaning of ḥarth is casting seed into the earth, and it was then applied, by way of metaphor (istiʿārah), to the fruits and benefits of deeds. The meaning is: whoever, by his deeds and earning, desires the reward of the Hereafter, Allah multiplies that for him, a good deed being rewarded tenfold up to seven hundred times over.

It was also said: its meaning is that He increases his success, his help, and the facilitation of the paths of good for him. ﴿And whoever desires the tilth of this world, We give him from it﴾, that is: whoever, by his deeds and earning, desires the reward of this world, which is its enjoyment, and what Allah provides His servants from it, We give him from it what Our will decrees and what is apportioned to him in Our decree.

Qatadah said: the meaning of ﴿We give him from it﴾ is: We ordain for him what has been apportioned to him, as in His words, ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will﴾ [al-Isra': 18]. Qatadah also said: Allah gives, out of the intention of the Hereafter, whatever of worldly affairs He wills, but He gives out of the intention of this world only the world. Al-Qushayri said: the apparent meaning is that the verse concerns the disbeliever, but this is a specification without a specifier (takhsīs bi-ghayr mukhassis).

Then He, glorified be He, explained that this one who intends the world by his deeds has no share in the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿And he has no share in the Hereafter﴾, because he did not work for the Hereafter, so there is no share for him in it. The interpretation of this verse has already been given in Surah al-Isra'.

﴿Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them in religion what Allah did not permit?﴾ When He, glorified be He, had explained the principle regarding the affairs of this world and the Hereafter, He followed it with an explanation of the great sin that necessitates the Fire. The hamzah is for the interrogation of affirmation and reproach. The pronoun in "shara'ū" refers to the partners, and the pronoun in "lahum" refers to the disbelievers, though it was also said the reverse, and the first is preferred.

The meaning of ﴿what Allah did not permit﴾ is what He did not permit of polytheism and sins. ﴿And had it not been for the decisive word﴾, which is the delay of their punishment, as in His words, ﴿Rather, the Hour is their appointed time﴾ [al-Qamar: 46], ﴿it would have been judged between them﴾ in this world, and they would have been hastened to punishment. The pronoun in "baynahum" refers either to the believers and the polytheists, or to the polytheists and their partners. ﴿And indeed the wrongdoers, for them is a painful punishment﴾, that is, the polytheists and the deniers, for them is a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter.

The majority read "wa-inna al-ẓālimīna" with a kasrah on the hamzah, as a resumed sentence (istiʾnāf, beginning a new clause). Muslim, al-A'raj and Ibn Hurmuz read it with a fatḥah on it, as a conjunction over "kalimat al-faṣl" (the decisive word).

﴿You will see the wrongdoers fearful of what they have earned﴾, that is: frightened and apprehensive of the evil deeds they earned, and that fear and apprehension will be on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And it will befall them﴾: the pronoun refers to "what they earned" with an elided noun in the construction, as al-Zajjaj said, that is: the recompense of what they earned will befall them and descend upon them without doubt, whether they feared it or not. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

Having mentioned the state of the wrongdoers, He mentioned the state of the believers, saying: ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds, in the meadows of the gardens﴾. Rawḍāt is the plural of rawḍah.

Abu Hayyan said: the common dialect is to pronounce the waw with a sukūn, while the dialect of Hudhayl pronounces it with a fatḥah. The rawḍah is a pleasant place abundant in greenery, and the explanation of this has already passed in Surah al-Rum. The rawḍah of Paradise is the finest of its dwellings, just as in this world it is the best of places. ﴿They will have whatever they wish with their Lord﴾ of kinds of blessings and types of delights. The governing element of "ʿinda rabbihim" is "yashāʾūna," or the governing element of "rawḍāt al-jannāt" is the stability (al-istiqrār). The indication by His words, "that" (dhālika), refers to what was mentioned before for the believers, and its predicate is the sentence mentioned after it, which is ﴿It is the great bounty﴾, that is, one that cannot be described and that minds cannot reach in knowing its reality.

The indication by His words, ﴿That is what Allah gives good news of to His servants﴾, refers to the great bounty, that is: He gives them the good news of it.

Then He described the servants by His words, ﴿Those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾. These are the ones who combine faith and action in accordance with what Allah commanded and abstaining from what He forbade, and they are the ones given that good news.

The majority read "yubashshiru" with shaddah, from "bashsharа". Mujahid and Humayd ibn Qays read it with a ḍammah on the initial letter, a sukūn on the bā', and a kasrah on the shīn, from "abshara". Some of the Seven read it with a fatḥah on the initial letter and a ḍammah on the shīn. The explanation of the readings for this word has already passed.

Then, when He, glorified be He, mentioned what He informed His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, of these noble rulings contained in His Book, He commanded him to inform them that he does not ask them for any reward for this conveyance. So He said: ﴿Say: I do not ask you any reward for it﴾, that is: say, O Muhammad: I do not seek from you any payment or benefit for conveying the message, ﴿except affection for the near of kin﴾. This exception may be connected (muttaṣil), meaning: except that you love me for my kinship among you, or love the people of my kin. It may also be disconnected (munqaṭiʿ).

Al-Zajjaj said: "illā al-mawaddah" is an exception that is not from the first, meaning: except that you love me for my kinship, so that you protect me. The address is to the Quraysh, and this is the view of Ikrimah, Mujahid, Abu Malik and al-Sha'bi. The meaning, on the disconnected reading, is: I do not ask you any reward at all, but I ask you for affection in the kinship that is between me and you. Respect me in it and do not hasten against me; leave me and the people. This was also the view of Qatadah, Muqatil, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and others, and it is the established view from Ibn ʿAbbas, as will come.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others said: they are the family of Muhammad. What those who hold this view cited as evidence will come.

Al-Hasan and others said: the meaning of the verse is: except seeking the love of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and drawing near to Him through obedience to Him.

Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said, and Ibn Jarir narrated it from al-Dahhak: this verse is abrogated (mansukh, superseded by a later ruling) and was revealed only in Mecca, when the polytheists were harming the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace. So Allah commanded them to show love to him. When he migrated, the Ansar sheltered him and supported him, and Allah then revealed to him: ﴿And I do not ask you any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 109], and He revealed to him: ﴿Say: Whatever reward I have asked of you is for yourselves; my reward is only from Allah﴾ [Saba': 47].

What will make the reward clear and the meaning of the verse manifest will come at the end of the discussion, if Allah wills.

﴿And whoever earns a good deed, We increase for him therein good﴾. The root of qarf is earning. It is said: "Fulan yaqrifu li-ʿiyālihi," meaning he earns for his dependants, and iqtirāf is earning, derived from their saying "rajul qirfah," when a man is cunning.

The meaning is: whoever earns a good deed, We increase for him this good deed in goodness by multiplying its reward.

Muqatil said: the meaning is: whoever earns a single good deed, We increase for him therein goodness, multiplying the single one tenfold or more.

It was also said: what is meant by this good deed is the affection for the near of kin, but applying it to the general sense is preferred, and the affection for the near of kin enters under it as a primary inclusion. ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾, that is: abundantly forgiving to the sinners, and abundantly appreciative to the obedient.

Qatadah said: "Forgiving of sins, Appreciative of good deeds." al-Suddi said: "Forgiving of the sins of the family of Muhammad."

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented a lie against Allah"?﴾ Am here is the disconnected (munqaṭiʿah) one, meaning: rather, do they say that Muhammad has fabricated a lie against Allah, by claiming prophethood? The denial is for rebuke. The meaning of fabricating a lie is inventing it.

Then He, glorified be He, answered their saying, saying: ﴿If Allah wills, He would seal over your heart﴾, that is: if he had fabricated a lie against Allah, He would have willed that it not come forth from him, and would have sealed upon his heart so that nothing of what he lied about would occur to his mind, as you claim.

Qatadah said: "He would seal over your heart, so He would make you forget the Qur'an." So He informed them that if he had fabricated against Him, He would have done to him what He informed them of in this verse. Mujahid and Muqatil said: "If He wills, He would bind your heart with patience regarding their harm, so that no hardship from their words enters your heart." It was also said: the address is to him, and what is meant is the disbelievers, that is: if He wills, He would seal the hearts of the disbelievers and hasten punishment upon them. This was mentioned by al-Qushayri.

It was also said: the meaning is: if your self had suggested to you to fabricate a lie against Allah, He would have sealed your heart, for no one dares to lie except one whose heart is sealed. The first view is preferred.

His words, ﴿And Allah will erase falsehood﴾, are a resumed sentence (istiʾnāf) that confirms what precedes it of the denial of fabrication. Ibn al-Anbari said: "yakhtim ʿalā qalbika" is a complete clause, meaning that what follows is a new sentence. Al-Kisa'i said: there is inversion (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr) in it, that is: and Allah erases falsehood. Al-Zajjaj said: "Am yaqūlūna iftarā ʿalā Allāhi kadhiban" is a complete clause.

His words, ﴿And Allah will erase falsehood﴾, are an argument against those who deny what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, brought, meaning: if what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, brought were false, He would have erased it, as His custom has been with fabricators. ﴿And establishes the truth through His words﴾, that is, Islam, and He makes it clear by His words, that is, by what He revealed of the Qur'an. ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾, aware of what is in the hearts of the servants. The waw in "wa-yamḥu" was dropped in some copies of the Qur'an, as al-Kisa'i related.

﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants﴾, that is: He accepts from the sinners among His servants their repentance to Him for the sins they committed and the evil deeds they earned. Repentance (tawbah) is regret over disobedience, with resolve not to return to it. It was also said: He accepts repentance from His friends and the people of His obedience. The first is preferred, for repentance is accepted from all servants, Muslim and disbeliever alike (p-1328), when it is sound, proceeding from sincerity of intention and sound resolve. ﴿And pardons evil deeds﴾ in general, for whoever repents of his evil deed. ﴿And He knows what you do﴾, of good and evil, and He will recompense each according to what he deserves.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read "tafʿalūna" with the second person (taʾ) as address. The rest read it with the third person (yāʾ) as narration. Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred the second reading, because this verb falls between two statements.

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds, He responds to them﴾. The relative pronoun is in the accusative position: Allah responds to those who believed and gives them what they asked of Him. It is said: "ajāba" and "istajāba" have the same meaning.

It was said: the meaning is that He accepts the worship of the sincere. It was also said that the implied sense is: "wa-yastajību lahum," so the lām was dropped, as it was dropped in His words, ﴿And when they measure for them﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 3], meaning "kālū lahum" (they measured for them). It was also said that the relative pronoun is in the nominative position, meaning: they respond to their Lord when He calls them, as in His words, ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you﴾ [al-Anfal: 24]. Al-Mubarrad said: the meaning of ﴿And those who believe respond﴾ is that those who believe seek a response; this is the true sense of the form istafʿala, so "alladhīna" is in the nominative position. The first is preferred.

﴿And He increases them from His bounty﴾, that is: He increases them beyond what they asked of Him, or beyond the reward they deserve, as a favour from Him. It was also said: He will grant them intercession for their brethren.

﴿And the disbelievers, for them is a severe punishment﴾. This is for the disbelievers, in contrast to what He mentioned for the believers before it.

﴿And if Allah were to extend provision to His servants, they would surely transgress in the earth﴾, that is: if Allah were to widen their provision, they would transgress in the earth, disobeying in it, being insolent toward the blessing, becoming arrogant, and seeking what is not theirs to seek. It was also said: the meaning is that if He made them equal in provision, some of them would not submit to others, and the crafts would cease. The first is preferred.

The apparent meaning is that it covers all kinds of provision. It has also been said that it refers specifically to rain. ﴿But He sends down in due measure what He wills.﴾ That is, He sends down provision to His servants in a measure according to His will and what His perfect wisdom requires. ﴿Indeed, He is Acquainted with His servants and Seeing﴾ of their conditions, and sees what is good for them, whether in expanding or restricting provision. So He decrees for each one of them what suits him and restrains him from corruption through transgression on the earth.

﴿And it is He who sends down the rain﴾ that is, the rain, which is the most beneficial kind of provision, the most widely useful, and the most productive of good. ﴿after they have despaired﴾ that is, after they have lost hope of it. Through this sending down of rain after despair, they will recognize the measure of His mercy toward them, and they will thank Him as thanks is due. ﴿And He is the Protecting Friend﴾ of His righteous servants, by doing good to them, bringing them benefits, and warding off harm from them, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, who deserves praise from them for His favors, both particular and general.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter﴾, that he said: "The life of the Hereafter." ﴿We will increase him in his tilth. And whoever desires the tilth of this world, We will give him of it﴾, to the end of the verse. He said: "Whoever prefers his worldly life over his Hereafter, Allah will not give him any share in the Hereafter except the Fire, and he will gain nothing from the world beyond provision that has already been finished and allotted to him."

Ahmad and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Hibban narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Give good news to this Ummah of elevation, high standing, victory, and establishment in the land, so long as they do not seek the world through the deeds of the Hereafter. Whoever among them does the deeds of the Hereafter for the sake of this world, he will have no share in the Hereafter."

al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter﴾, to the end of the verse, and then said: 'Allah says: O son of Adam, devote yourself to My worship, and I will fill your heart with richness and close off your poverty.
