﴿And those who avoid the major sins and the immoralities﴾. The relative pronoun is in the genitive position, coordinated with "those who believe," or a substitute for it, or in the accusative position with an implied "I mean"; the first is preferable. The meaning is: what is with God is better and more lasting for those who believe and for those who avoid.

What is meant by ﴿the major sins of sin﴾ is the major sins among the sins, and we have already established their verification in Surat al-Nisa'.

The majority read "kabā'ir" in the plural, and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "kabīr" in the singular, and it conveys the meaning of the plural, because the genitive construction is generic, like the definite article.

The "fawāḥish" (immoralities) are among the major sins, but with the description of being an immorality they are as if above them, such as murder and fornication and the like. Muqatil said: the immoralities are the causes of the prescribed punishments (mūjibāt al-ḥudūd).

Al-Suddi said: they are fornication.

﴿And when they become angry, they forgive﴾, meaning: they overlook the sin that angered them, restrain their rage, and bear with those who wronged them. Anger was singled out for forgiveness because its dominance over human nature and its overpowering of him is severe, so no one forgives at the surge of anger except one whom God has expanded his chest for and specially favored with the quality of forbearance. For this reason God (glory be to Him) praised them in Al 'Imran by His saying: ﴿And those who restrain their anger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134].

Ibn Zayd said: God made the believers of two kinds: a kind who pardon their wrongdoers, and He began with mentioning them, and a kind who take vengeance on their wrongdoers, and they are those whose mention will come.

﴿And those who respond to their Lord and establish the prayer﴾, meaning: they answered Him in what He called them to, and they upheld what He made obligatory upon them of the obligatory prayer.

Ibn Zayd said: They are the Ansar in Medina, who responded to faith in the Messenger when he sent to them twelve chiefs (naqībs) from among them before the Hijrah, and they established the prayer at its appointed times with its conditions and its forms.

﴿And their affair is by consultation among them﴾, meaning: they consult one another and do not hasten nor act alone in opinion. The word "shūrā" is a verbal noun from "shāwartuhu," like "bushrā" and "dhikrā."

al-Dahhak said: It is their consultation when they heard of the emergence of the Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family and grant him peace) and the arrival of the chiefs to them, when their opinion gathered in the house of Abu Ayyub upon faith in him and support for him.

It was said: what is meant is their consulting in every matter that presents itself to them, so none of them singles out an opinion over the others. How excellent is what Bashshar ibn Burd said:

When opinion reaches the point where consultation is needed, seek help
from the opinion of a sincere advisor or the counsel of a prudent man.
And do not make consultation a burden upon you, for the wing-feathers of a bird are the strength of its primary flight feathers.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 42, verse 29–43 (part 2 of 2):

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to consult his companions in his affairs, and Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to do so, saying: ﴿And consult them in the matter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. We have already discussed consultation (shura) in the commentary on Al 'Imran.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾, i.e., they spend it in the way of good and give charity from it to the needy.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the group that seeks to defend itself against one who wronged it, saying: ﴿And those who, when an oppression afflicts them, they defend themselves﴾. That is, when the oppression of one who oppresses them without right afflicts them. He, glorified is He, mentioned these defenders in the context of praise, just as He mentioned forgiveness at the time of anger in the context of praise, because humbling oneself before the oppressor is not among the attributes of one to whom Allah has given honour, as He said: ﴿And to Allah belongs honour, and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [Al-Munafiqun: 8]. So defending oneself when oppressed is a virtue, just as pardoning at the time of anger is a virtue.

Al-Nakha'i said: "They used to dislike to humiliate themselves, lest the foolish become bold against them."

However, this self-defence is conditional upon confining oneself to what Allah has permitted to him and not exceeding it, as He, glorified is He, explained right after this with His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. So He, glorified is He, made clear that justice in self-defence is to be limited to equivalence. The apparent meaning of this is generality.

Muqatil, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and Sufyan said: this is specific to the one who has been wounded, who may take retaliation from the wounder by way of qisas (retribution), and not otherwise.

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: it is the response to the abusive person when he says, "May Allah disgrace you," so he says, "May Allah disgrace you," without transgressing. Calling the recompense an "evil" is either because it harms the one upon whom it falls, or by way of mushakalah (correspondence in wording), due to the similarity of the two in form.

Then, when He, glorified is He, made clear that the recompense of an evil by its like is a permissible right, He explained the virtue of pardon, saying: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah﴾. That is, whoever pardons one who wronged him and makes reconciliation through the pardon between himself and his oppressor, i.e., Allah, glorified is He, will reward him for that. The reward is left indefinite to magnify its importance and to draw attention to its greatness.

Muqatil said: "So pardon is among the righteous deeds." We have already explained this in the surah of Al 'Imran.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the wrongdoers' departure from His love, which is the cause of success and salvation, saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who initiate wrongdoing. Muqatil said: "He means whoever begins with wrongdoing," and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said the same. It was also said: He does not love whoever exceeds the limit in retaliation and goes beyond the bound in it, because going beyond is wrongdoing.

﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾: this is a verbal noun (masdar) added to its object, i.e., after the wrongdoer had wronged him. The lam is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is the lam of oath, but the first is preferable. The "man" (مَن) is conditional, and its answer is: ﴿those — there is no route (sabil) against them﴾, i.e., no blame or punishment. It is also permissible that "man" be a relative pronoun (al-mawsulah), and the fa' has entered its answer, making the relative pronoun resemble the conditional; but the first is preferable.

When He, glorified is He, negated the route against whoever (p-1332) defends himself after being wronged, He made clear upon whom the route falls, saying: 42 ﴿The route is only against those who wrong people﴾, i.e., who transgress against them initially. So said most of the scholars.

Ibn Jurayj said: i.e., they wrong them by associating partners with Allah, which opposes their religion. ﴿And they commit injustice on the earth without right﴾, i.e., they act against lives and property without right. So said most of the scholars.

Muqatil said: their transgression is their doing of acts of disobedience. It was also said: they act arrogantly and tyrannically.

Abu Malik said: it is what the people of Mecca hoped, that a religion other than Islam would prevail in Mecca. The indication by His saying "those" (أُولَئِكَ) refers to "those who wrong people," and it is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is: ﴿for them is a painful punishment﴾, i.e., for them, by this cause, is a punishment of severe pain.

Then He, glorified is He, encouraged patience and pardon, saying: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives﴾, i.e., is patient over harm and forgives the one who wronged him and does not retaliate. The discussion of this lam and "man" is like the discussion of ﴿and whoever defends himself﴾, that indeed such patience and forgiveness are ﴿of the determined matters (min 'azm al-umur)﴾, i.e., that this is from it, and it was elided for its clarity, as in their saying: "Ghee is two manwas for a dirham."

Muqatil said: "among the matters which Allah has commanded." Al-Zajjaj said: "The patient one is given his patience as a reward, so desire for the reward is more complete in determination." Ibn Zayd said: all of this is abrogated (mansukh) by jihad, and that it is specific to the polytheists.

Qatadah said: it is general, and this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'anic composition. ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾, i.e., for him there is no one after Him who guides him or helps him. The apparent meaning of the verse is generality. It was also said: it is specific to whoever turned away from the Prophet (ﷺ) and did not act upon what he called him to of faith in Allah and acting upon what He legislated. The first is preferable.

Ahmad, Ibn Rahawayh, Ibn Mani', 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim have narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "Shall I inform you of the best verse in the Book of Allah, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related to us: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you, it is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾. I will explain it to you, O 'Ali: whatever affliction, illness, punishment or trial in this world befalls you is because of what your hands have earned; and Allah is too Generous to repeat the punishment upon you in the Hereafter, and what Allah has pardoned in this world, Allah is too Generous to return to it after His pardon."

'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No servant is struck by a calamity, whether great or small, except because of a sin, and what Allah pardons is more numerous." And he recited: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you﴾, the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Kaffarat, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from 'Imran ibn Husayn that some of his companions entered upon him while he had been afflicted in his body, and said: "We are truly distressed for you because of what we see in you." He said: "Do not be distressed by what you see, for what you see is due to a sin, and what Allah pardons is more numerous." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you﴾ to its end.

Ahmad narrated from Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Nothing afflicts the believer in his body, harming him, except that Allah expiates his sins by it."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Bara' who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A slip of the foot, a twitch of a vein, or a scratch of a stick is only because of what your hands have sent forth, and what Allah pardons is more."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿so they remain still upon its back﴾, he said: "They move but do not run in the sea."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿still (rawakid)﴾, he said: "Standing still, or He destroys them," meaning He destroys them.

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'ishah, who said: Zaynab entered upon me while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was with me, and she turned toward me and abused me. The Prophet (ﷺ) restrained her, but she did not stop, so he said to me: "Abuse her." So I abused her until her saliva dried in her mouth, and the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brightened with joy.

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Of two people who revile each other, whatever they say falls upon the one who initiated it, unless the wronged one exceeds the limit." Then he recited: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will command a herald to call out: 'Let whoever has a reward upon Allah stand up.' None will stand except those who pardoned in the world, and that is His saying: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah﴾."

al-Bayhaqi narrated from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "A caller will call out: 'Whoever has a reward upon Allah, let him enter Paradise,' twice, and whoever pardoned his brother will stand up. Allah said: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah﴾."

He (glory be to Him) mentioned some of His signs that demonstrate the perfection of His power, which necessitates His oneness and the truth of what He promised concerning resurrection. He said: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning, their creation in this wondrous manner and with this strange craftsmanship. ﴿And the living creatures He has dispersed in both﴾ may be connected to "creation," and it may be connected to "the heavens." The "dābba" (living creature) is the name for everything that crawls.

Al-Farra' said: He meant what He dispersed in the earth without the heaven, as in His saying: ﴿From them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], and they only emerge from the salt water and not from the sweet.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: Its estimated meaning is "and what He dispersed in one of the two," so the genitive noun was omitted.

Mujahid said: This includes the angels and the humans, and God Most High has said: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾ [al-Naml: 8]. ﴿And He is, when He wills, over their gathering﴾, meaning, their assembling (ḥashr) on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿competent﴾. The temporal clause is connected to "their gathering," not to "competent." Abu al-Baqa' said: because otherwise it would result in: "He is competent over their gathering when He wills," so that power would be linked to will, and that is impossible.

Shihab al-Din said: I do not know what makes it impossible according to the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah. If he is speaking according to the view of the Mu'tazilah, namely that power relates to what God did not will, then his statement stands, but that is a corrupt doctrine that is not permissible to hold.

﴿And whatever affliction befalls you, it is for what your hands have earned﴾, meaning: whatever afflictions befall you, whatever they may be, it is because of what your hands have earned of sins.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "bimā kasabat" without the fa', and the rest read it with the fa'. The "mā" in ﴿wa-mā aṣābakum﴾ is conditional (shartiyyah), and for this reason the fa' entered its response according to the reading of the majority. Its omission is not permissible according to Sibawayh and the majority. Al-Akhfash permitted the omission, as in His saying: ﴿And if you obey them, you are indeed polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 121], and in the words of the poet:

Whoever does good deeds, God will reward them,
and evil with evil, with God, is like for like.

It was also said that it is the relative (mawsulah) "mā," and then both omission and inclusion would be permissible, but the first is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: Including the fa' is better, because the fa' is the apodosis (mujāzāt jawāb al-shart) of the conditional. Whoever omits the fa' does so on the basis that "mā" means "alladhī" (that which), and the meaning is: "That which afflicted you occurred because of what your hands have earned."

Al-Hasan said: The affliction here refers to the prescribed punishments (ḥudūd) for sins. But the preferable view is to take it in its generality, as indicated by the indefinite noun occurring in a negative context and the inclusion of "min" (of) as expressing totality on it. ﴿And He pardons much﴾ of the sins which the servants commit, so He does not punish for them. The meaning of the verse is that He expiates for the servant by means of the afflictions that befall him, and pardons much of the sins.

Sound evidences have established that everything a person is afflicted with in this world is either rewarded for him or expiated from his sins.

It was also said that this verse is specific to the disbelievers, in the sense that what they are afflicted with is because of their sins, without that being an expiation for a sin or an acquisition of reward, and that their punishment is left aside for much of their sins, so He does not hasten to punish them in this world but gives them respite until the Last Abode.

The preferable view is to take the verse in its generality, and pardon (ʿafw) applies both to the postponement of punishment and to the erasure of the sin and the lifting of address (khiṭāb) concerning it.

Al-Wahidi said: This is the most hopeful (arjā) verse in the Book of God, because He made the sins of the believers of two kinds: one kind He expiates from them through afflictions, and another kind He pardons in this world, and He is Generous and does not retract His pardon. This is the custom of God with the believers.

As for the disbeliever, his sin is not hastened in punishment for him until he is brought to account for it on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And you cannot escape in the earth﴾, meaning: you cannot flee from it by fleeing in the earth or in the heaven, even if you were in them; rather, what He has decreed upon them of afflictions befalls them and descends upon them. ﴿And you have no protector other than God﴾ who would support you and thereby avert what God has decreed, ﴿nor any helper who would help you against the punishment of God, in this world or in the Hereafter.﴾

Then He (glory be to Him) mentioned another of His great signs, which demonstrate His oneness and the truth of what He promised, and He said: ﴿And among His signs are the ships﴾. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "al-jawārī" with the "yā'" affirmed when connected; when stopping, its affirmation is according to the original form and its omission is for lightening. They are the ships, the singular of which is "jāriyah," meaning "sailing," ﴿on the sea like mountains﴾, meaning like the mountains, the plural of "'alam," which is a mountain. From it is the saying of al-Khansa':

Indeed Sakhr, the guided ones take him as a guide,
as if he were a beacon with fire on its summit.

Al-Khalil said: Everything elevated among the Arabs is an "'alam." Mujahid said: "al-a'lām" are palaces, whose singular is "'alam."

﴿If He wills, He calms the wind﴾. The majority read "yashā'" with a hamzah, and Warsh from Nafi' read it without a hamzah. The majority read "al-rīḥ" in the singular, and Nafi' read "al-riyāḥ" in the plural, meaning: He calms the wind by which the ships sail, ﴿so they remain motionless (fa-yaẓlalna)﴾, meaning, the ships become stationary, still, fixed, ﴿upon its back﴾, the back of the sea.

It is said: "rakada al-mā'u rukūdan" meaning the water became still; likewise "rakadat al-rīḥ" and "rakadat al-safīnah," and everything fixed in a place is "rākid."

The majority read "fa-yaẓlalna" with the first lām pronounced with a fatha, and Qatadah read it with a kasra, which is a rare dialect.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, that which has been mentioned of the matter of the ships, there are signs, great proofs, ﴿for every steadfast, grateful person﴾, meaning, for everyone who is greatly patient in trials and greatly thankful for blessings.

Qutrub said: "al-Ṣabbār" is the one who is very grateful, who when he is given, gives thanks, and when he is tested, is patient.

'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah said:

How many a person blessed who is not grateful,
and how many a person tested who is not patient.

﴿Or He destroys them for what they have earned﴾: it is coordinated with "yuskin" (He calms), meaning He destroys them by drowning, and what is meant is that He destroys them for what they have earned of sins.

It was also said: for what they associated (with Him).

The first is preferable, for He destroys in the sea both the polytheist and the non-polytheist. It is said: "awbaqahu," meaning he destroyed him. ﴿And He pardons much﴾ of its people by overlooking their sins, so He saves them from drowning.

The majority read "yaʿfu" in the jussive, coordinated with the response of the conditional. Al-Qushayri said: There is a problem with this reading, because the meaning would be: "If He wills, He calms the wind, so those ships remain stationary, or He destroys them for the sins of their people." It is not good to coordinate "yaʿfu" with this, because the meaning would become: "If He wills, He pardons," and that is not the meaning. Rather the meaning is the report of pardon without a condition of will. So it is coordinated with the jussive in form, not in meaning. Some read "wa-yaʿfū" with the nominative, and it is good in meaning.

Abu Hayyan said: What he said is not good, since the meaning of the construction is not understood. The meaning is: only that He, Most High, destroyed some people and saved others by way of pardoning them. Al-A'mash read "wa-yaʿfū" with the nominative. Some people of Medina read it in the accusative, with "an" implied after the "wa," as in the saying of al-Nabighah:

If Abu Qabus perishes, the spring of the people will perish, and the sacred month,
and we will take after him by the tails of a life, a back thin of hump, without a hump.

With the accusative of "wa-na'khudha."

﴿And that those who dispute concerning Our signs may know that they have no escape﴾. The majority read "yaʿlam" in the accusative. Al-Zajjaj said: "ʿalā al-ṣarf." He said: The meaning of "ṣarf" is turning the coordination from the wording to the coordination with the meaning. He said: Because it was not good to coordinate "wa-yaʿlam" as jussive with what precedes it, since the meaning would be "if He wills with knowledge," he turned to coordinating it with the verbal noun (maṣdar) of the verb that precedes it, and that is only possible by implying "an," so that it with the verb becomes in the sense of a noun. And from this are the two verses of al-Nabighah mentioned shortly before. As al-Zajjaj said, al-Mubarrad and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said that, but this view has been objected to with things of no value.

It was also said: the accusative is by coordination on a deleted causal clause, and the estimated meaning is: "so that He may take vengeance on them and know."

Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that what follows from the condition is the destruction of some people and the salvation of others, so it is not good to estimate "so that He may take vengeance on them."

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "yaʿlamu" in the nominative, as a resumptive (isti'nāf) clause. This reading is clear in meaning and plain in wording.

It was also read in the jussive, coordinated with the preceding jussive, meaning: "And if He wills, He combines between destruction, salvation, and warning."

The meaning of ﴿they have no escape﴾ is that they have no flight and no refuge, as said by Qutrub.

al-Suddi said: They have no refuge, and it is derived from the saying of the people: "ḥāṣa bihi al-baʿīr ḥaysatan," when the camel threw him off, and from it the saying: "Fulan yaḥīṣu ʿan al-ḥaqq," meaning he swerves away from it.

﴿So whatever you have been given of a thing is an enjoyment of the life of this world﴾. When He (glory be to Him) mentioned the proofs of oneness, He mentioned the warning against this world, meaning: whatever you have been given of wealth and abundance in provision is only a little enjoyment for a few days, which passes and goes away.

Then He encouraged them toward the reward of the Hereafter and what is with God of lasting bliss, and He said: ﴿And what is with God is better and more lasting﴾, meaning: what is with God of reward for acts of obedience and recompense for them with the gardens is better than the enjoyment of this world and more lasting, because it is everlasting and does not end, while the enjoyment of this world ends quickly.

Then He (glory be to Him) explained for whom this is, and He said: ﴿For those who believe﴾, meaning: who are truthful and act according to what faith requires, ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾, meaning: they entrust their affairs to Him and depend upon Him in all their matters, not upon other than Him.

﴿And those who avoid the major sins and the immoralities﴾. The relative pronoun is in the genitive position, coordinated with "those who believe," or a substitute for it, or in the accusative position with an implied "I mean"; the first is preferable. The meaning is: what is with God is better and more lasting for those who believe and for those who avoid.

What is meant by ﴿the major sins of sin﴾ is the major sins among the sins, and we have already established their verification in Surat al-Nisa'.

The majority read "kabā'ir" in the plural, and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "kabīr" in the singular, and it conveys the meaning of the plural, because the genitive construction is generic, like the definite article.

The "fawāḥish" (immoralities) are among the major sins, but with the description of being an immorality they are as if above them, such as murder and fornication and the like. Muqatil said: the immoralities are the causes of the prescribed punishments (mūjibāt al-ḥudūd).

Al-Suddi said: they are fornication.

﴿And when they become angry, they forgive﴾, meaning: they overlook the sin that angered them, restrain their rage, and bear with those who wronged them. Anger was singled out for forgiveness because its dominance over human nature and its overpowering of him is severe, so no one forgives at the surge of anger except one whom God has expanded his chest for and specially favored with the quality of forbearance. For this reason God (glory be to Him) praised them in Al 'Imran by His saying: ﴿And those who restrain their anger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134].

Ibn Zayd said: God made the believers of two kinds: a kind who pardon their wrongdoers, and He began with mentioning them, and a kind who take vengeance on their wrongdoers, and they are those whose mention will come.

﴿And those who respond to their Lord and establish the prayer﴾, meaning: they answered Him in what He called them to, and they upheld what He made obligatory upon them of the obligatory prayer.

Ibn Zayd said: They are the Ansar in Medina, who responded to faith in the Messenger when he sent to them twelve chiefs (naqībs) from among them before the Hijrah, and they established the prayer at its appointed times with its conditions and its forms.

﴿And their affair is by consultation among them﴾, meaning: they consult one another and do not hasten nor act alone in opinion. The word "shūrā" is a verbal noun from "shāwartuhu," like "bushrā" and "dhikrā."

al-Dahhak said: It is their consultation when they heard of the emergence of the Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family and grant him peace) and the arrival of the chiefs to them, when their opinion gathered in the house of Abu Ayyub upon faith in him and support for him.

It was said: what is meant is their consulting in every matter that presents itself to them, so none of them singles out an opinion over the others. How excellent is what Bashshar ibn Burd said:

When opinion reaches the point where consultation is needed, seek help
from the opinion of a sincere advisor or the counsel of a prudent man.
And do not make consultation a burden upon you, for the wing-feathers of a bird are the strength of its primary flight feathers.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 42, verse 29–43 (part 2 of 2):

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to consult his companions in his affairs, and Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to do so, saying: ﴿And consult them in the matter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. We have already discussed consultation (shura) in the commentary on Al 'Imran.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾, i.e., they spend it in the way of good and give charity from it to the needy.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the group that seeks to defend itself against one who wronged it, saying: ﴿And those who, when an oppression afflicts them, they defend themselves﴾. That is, when the oppression of one who oppresses them without right afflicts them. He, glorified is He, mentioned these defenders in the context of praise, just as He mentioned forgiveness at the time of anger in the context of praise, because humbling oneself before the oppressor is not among the attributes of one to whom Allah has given honour, as He said: ﴿And to Allah belongs honour, and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [Al-Munafiqun: 8]. So defending oneself when oppressed is a virtue, just as pardoning at the time of anger is a virtue.

Al-Nakha'i said: "They used to dislike to humiliate themselves, lest the foolish become bold against them."

However, this self-defence is conditional upon confining oneself to what Allah has permitted to him and not exceeding it, as He, glorified is He, explained right after this with His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. So He, glorified is He, made clear that justice in self-defence is to be limited to equivalence. The apparent meaning of this is generality.

Muqatil, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and Sufyan said: this is specific to the one who has been wounded, who may take retaliation from the wounder by way of qisas (retribution), and not otherwise.

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: it is the response to the abusive person when he says, "May Allah disgrace you," so he says, "May Allah disgrace you," without transgressing. Calling the recompense an "evil" is either because it harms the one upon whom it falls, or by way of mushakalah (correspondence in wording), due to the similarity of the two in form.

Then, when He, glorified is He, made clear that the recompense of an evil by its like is a permissible right, He explained the virtue of pardon, saying: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah﴾. That is, whoever pardons one who wronged him and makes reconciliation through the pardon between himself and his oppressor, i.e., Allah, glorified is He, will reward him for that. The reward is left indefinite to magnify its importance and to draw attention to its greatness.

Muqatil said: "So pardon is among the righteous deeds." We have already explained this in the surah of Al 'Imran.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the wrongdoers' departure from His love, which is the cause of success and salvation, saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who initiate wrongdoing. Muqatil said: "He means whoever begins with wrongdoing," and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said the same. It was also said: He does not love whoever exceeds the limit in retaliation and goes beyond the bound in it, because going beyond is wrongdoing.

﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾: this is a verbal noun (masdar) added to its object, i.e., after the wrongdoer had wronged him. The lam is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is the lam of oath, but the first is preferable. The "man" (مَن) is conditional, and its answer is: ﴿those — there is no route (sabil) against them﴾, i.e., no blame or punishment. It is also permissible that "man" be a relative pronoun (al-mawsulah), and the fa' has entered its answer, making the relative pronoun resemble the conditional; but the first is preferable.

When He, glorified is He, negated the route against whoever (p-1332) defends himself after being wronged, He made clear upon whom the route falls, saying: 42 ﴿The route is only against those who wrong people﴾, i.e., who transgress against them initially. So said most of the scholars.

Ibn Jurayj said: i.e., they wrong them by associating partners with Allah, which opposes their religion. ﴿And they commit injustice on the earth without right﴾, i.e., they act against lives and property without right. So said most of the scholars.

Muqatil said: their transgression is their doing of acts of disobedience. It was also said: they act arrogantly and tyrannically.

Abu Malik said: it is what the people of Mecca hoped, that a religion other than Islam would prevail in Mecca. The indication by His saying "those" (أُولَئِكَ) refers to "those who wrong people," and it is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is: ﴿for them is a painful punishment﴾, i.e., for them, by this cause, is a punishment of severe pain.

Then He, glorified is He, encouraged patience and pardon, saying: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives﴾, i.e., is patient over harm and forgives the one who wronged him and does not retaliate. The discussion of this lam and "man" is like the discussion of ﴿and whoever defends himself﴾, that indeed such patience and forgiveness are ﴿of the determined matters (min 'azm al-umur)﴾, i.e., that this is from it, and it was elided for its clarity, as in their saying: "Ghee is two manwas for a dirham."

Muqatil said: "among the matters which Allah has commanded." Al-Zajjaj said: "The patient one is given his patience as a reward, so desire for the reward is more complete in determination." Ibn Zayd said: all of this is abrogated (mansukh) by jihad, and that it is specific to the polytheists.

Qatadah said: it is general, and this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'anic composition. ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾, i.e., for him there is no one after Him who guides him or helps him. The apparent meaning of the verse is generality. It was also said: it is specific to whoever turned away from the Prophet (ﷺ) and did not act upon what he called him to of faith in Allah and acting upon what He legislated. The first is preferable.

Ahmad, Ibn Rahawayh, Ibn Mani', 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim have narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "Shall I inform you of the best verse in the Book of Allah, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related to us: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you, it is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾. I will explain it to you, O 'Ali: whatever affliction, illness, punishment or trial in this world befalls you is because of what your hands have earned; and Allah is too Generous to repeat the punishment upon you in the Hereafter, and what Allah has pardoned in this world, Allah is too Generous to return to it after His pardon."

'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No servant is struck by a calamity, whether great or small, except because of a sin, and what Allah pardons is more numerous." And he recited: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you﴾, the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Kaffarat, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from 'Imran ibn Husayn that some of his companions entered upon him while he had been afflicted in his body, and said: "We are truly distressed for you because of what we see in you." He said: "Do not be distressed by what you see, for what you see is due to a sin, and what Allah pardons is more numerous." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you﴾ to its end.

Ahmad narrated from Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Nothing afflicts the believer in his body, harming him, except that Allah expiates his sins by it."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Bara' who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A slip of the foot, a twitch of a vein, or a scratch of a stick is only because of what your hands have sent forth, and what Allah pardons is more."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿so they remain still upon its back﴾, he said: "They move but do not run in the sea."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿still (rawakid)﴾, he said: "Standing still, or He destroys them," meaning He destroys them.

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'ishah, who said: Zaynab entered upon me while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was with me, and she turned toward me and abused me. The Prophet (ﷺ) restrained her, but she did not stop, so he said to me: "Abuse her." So I abused her until her saliva dried in her mouth, and the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brightened with joy.

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Of two people who revile each other, whatever they say falls upon the one who initiated it, unless the wronged one exceeds the limit." Then he recited: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will command a herald to call out: 'Let whoever has a reward upon Allah stand up.' None will stand except those who pardoned in the world, and that is His saying: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah﴾."

al-Bayhaqi narrated from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "A caller will call out: 'Whoever has a reward upon Allah, let him enter Paradise,' twice, and whoever pardoned his brother will stand up. Allah said: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah﴾."

He (glory be to Him) mentioned some of His signs that demonstrate the perfection of His power, which necessitates His oneness and the truth of what He promised concerning resurrection. He said: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning, their creation in this wondrous manner and with this strange craftsmanship. ﴿And the living creatures He has dispersed in both﴾ may be connected to "creation," and it may be connected to "the heavens." The "dābba" (living creature) is the name for everything that crawls.

Al-Farra' said: He meant what He dispersed in the earth without the heaven, as in His saying: ﴿From them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], and they only emerge from the salt water and not from the sweet.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: Its estimated meaning is "and what He dispersed in one of the two," so the genitive noun was omitted.

Mujahid said: This includes the angels and the humans, and God Most High has said: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾ [al-Naml: 8]. ﴿And He is, when He wills, over their gathering﴾, meaning, their assembling (ḥashr) on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿competent﴾. The temporal clause is connected to "their gathering," not to "competent." Abu al-Baqa' said: because otherwise it would result in: "He is competent over their gathering when He wills," so that power would be linked to will, and that is impossible.

Shihab al-Din said: I do not know what makes it impossible according to the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah. If he is speaking according to the view of the Mu'tazilah, namely that power relates to what God did not will, then his statement stands, but that is a corrupt doctrine that is not permissible to hold.

﴿And whatever affliction befalls you, it is for what your hands have earned﴾, meaning: whatever afflictions befall you, whatever they may be, it is because of what your hands have earned of sins.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "bimā kasabat" without the fa', and the rest read it with the fa'. The "mā" in ﴿wa-mā aṣābakum﴾ is conditional (shartiyyah), and for this reason the fa' entered its response according to the reading of the majority. Its omission is not permissible according to Sibawayh and the majority. Al-Akhfash permitted the omission, as in His saying: ﴿And if you obey them, you are indeed polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 121], and in the words of the poet:

Whoever does good deeds, God will reward them,
and evil with evil, with God, is like for like.

It was also said that it is the relative (mawsulah) "mā," and then both omission and inclusion would be permissible, but the first is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: Including the fa' is better, because the fa' is the apodosis (mujāzāt jawāb al-shart) of the conditional. Whoever omits the fa' does so on the basis that "mā" means "alladhī" (that which), and the meaning is: "That which afflicted you occurred because of what your hands have earned."

Al-Hasan said: The affliction here refers to the prescribed punishments (ḥudūd) for sins. But the preferable view is to take it in its generality, as indicated by the indefinite noun occurring in a negative context and the inclusion of "min" (of) as expressing totality on it. ﴿And He pardons much﴾ of the sins which the servants commit, so He does not punish for them. The meaning of the verse is that He expiates for the servant by means of the afflictions that befall him, and pardons much of the sins.

Sound evidences have established that everything a person is afflicted with in this world is either rewarded for him or expiated from his sins.

It was also said that this verse is specific to the disbelievers, in the sense that what they are afflicted with is because of their sins, without that being an expiation for a sin or an acquisition of reward, and that their punishment is left aside for much of their sins, so He does not hasten to punish them in this world but gives them respite until the Last Abode.

The preferable view is to take the verse in its generality, and pardon (ʿafw) applies both to the postponement of punishment and to the erasure of the sin and the lifting of address (khiṭāb) concerning it.

Al-Wahidi said: This is the most hopeful (arjā) verse in the Book of God, because He made the sins of the believers of two kinds: one kind He expiates from them through afflictions, and another kind He pardons in this world, and He is Generous and does not retract His pardon. This is the custom of God with the believers.

As for the disbeliever, his sin is not hastened in punishment for him until he is brought to account for it on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And you cannot escape in the earth﴾, meaning: you cannot flee from it by fleeing in the earth or in the heaven, even if you were in them; rather, what He has decreed upon them of afflictions befalls them and descends upon them. ﴿And you have no protector other than God﴾ who would support you and thereby avert what God has decreed, ﴿nor any helper who would help you against the punishment of God, in this world or in the Hereafter.﴾

Then He (glory be to Him) mentioned another of His great signs, which demonstrate His oneness and the truth of what He promised, and He said: ﴿And among His signs are the ships﴾. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "al-jawārī" with the "yā'" affirmed when connected; when stopping, its affirmation is according to the original form and its omission is for lightening. They are the ships, the singular of which is "jāriyah," meaning "sailing," ﴿on the sea like mountains﴾, meaning like the mountains, the plural of "'alam," which is a mountain. From it is the saying of al-Khansa':

Indeed Sakhr, the guided ones take him as a guide,
as if he were a beacon with fire on its summit.

Al-Khalil said: Everything elevated among the Arabs is an "'alam." Mujahid said: "al-a'lām" are palaces, whose singular is "'alam."

﴿If He wills, He calms the wind﴾. The majority read "yashā'" with a hamzah, and Warsh from Nafi' read it without a hamzah. The majority read "al-rīḥ" in the singular, and Nafi' read "al-riyāḥ" in the plural, meaning: He calms the wind by which the ships sail, ﴿so they remain motionless (fa-yaẓlalna)﴾, meaning, the ships become stationary, still, fixed, ﴿upon its back﴾, the back of the sea.

It is said: "rakada al-mā'u rukūdan" meaning the water became still; likewise "rakadat al-rīḥ" and "rakadat al-safīnah," and everything fixed in a place is "rākid."

The majority read "fa-yaẓlalna" with the first lām pronounced with a fatha, and Qatadah read it with a kasra, which is a rare dialect.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, that which has been mentioned of the matter of the ships, there are signs, great proofs, ﴿for every steadfast, grateful person﴾, meaning, for everyone who is greatly patient in trials and greatly thankful for blessings.

Qutrub said: "al-Ṣabbār" is the one who is very grateful, who when he is given, gives thanks, and when he is tested, is patient.

'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah said:

How many a person blessed who is not grateful,
and how many a person tested who is not patient.

﴿Or He destroys them for what they have earned﴾: it is coordinated with "yuskin" (He calms), meaning He destroys them by drowning, and what is meant is that He destroys them for what they have earned of sins.

It was also said: for what they associated (with Him).

The first is preferable, for He destroys in the sea both the polytheist and the non-polytheist. It is said: "awbaqahu," meaning he destroyed him. ﴿And He pardons much﴾ of its people by overlooking their sins, so He saves them from drowning.

The majority read "yaʿfu" in the jussive, coordinated with the response of the conditional. Al-Qushayri said: There is a problem with this reading, because the meaning would be: "If He wills, He calms the wind, so those ships remain stationary, or He destroys them for the sins of their people." It is not good to coordinate "yaʿfu" with this, because the meaning would become: "If He wills, He pardons," and that is not the meaning. Rather the meaning is the report of pardon without a condition of will. So it is coordinated with the jussive in form, not in meaning. Some read "wa-yaʿfū" with the nominative, and it is good in meaning.

Abu Hayyan said: What he said is not good, since the meaning of the construction is not understood. The meaning is: only that He, Most High, destroyed some people and saved others by way of pardoning them. Al-A'mash read "wa-yaʿfū" with the nominative. Some people of Medina read it in the accusative, with "an" implied after the "wa," as in the saying of al-Nabighah:

If Abu Qabus perishes, the spring of the people will perish, and the sacred month,
and we will take after him by the tails of a life, a back thin of hump, without a hump.

With the accusative of "wa-na'khudha."

﴿And that those who dispute concerning Our signs may know that they have no escape﴾. The majority read "yaʿlam" in the accusative. Al-Zajjaj said: "ʿalā al-ṣarf." He said: The meaning of "ṣarf" is turning the coordination from the wording to the coordination with the meaning. He said: Because it was not good to coordinate "wa-yaʿlam" as jussive with what precedes it, since the meaning would be "if He wills with knowledge," he turned to coordinating it with the verbal noun (maṣdar) of the verb that precedes it, and that is only possible by implying "an," so that it with the verb becomes in the sense of a noun. And from this are the two verses of al-Nabighah mentioned shortly before. As al-Zajjaj said, al-Mubarrad and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said that, but this view has been objected to with things of no value.

It was also said: the accusative is by coordination on a deleted causal clause, and the estimated meaning is: "so that He may take vengeance on them and know."

Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that what follows from the condition is the destruction of some people and the salvation of others, so it is not good to estimate "so that He may take vengeance on them."

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "yaʿlamu" in the nominative, as a resumptive (isti'nāf) clause. This reading is clear in meaning and plain in wording.

It was also read in the jussive, coordinated with the preceding jussive, meaning: "And if He wills, He combines between destruction, salvation, and warning."

The meaning of ﴿they have no escape﴾ is that they have no flight and no refuge, as said by Qutrub.

al-Suddi said: They have no refuge, and it is derived from the saying of the people: "ḥāṣa bihi al-baʿīr ḥaysatan," when the camel threw him off, and from it the saying: "Fulan yaḥīṣu ʿan al-ḥaqq," meaning he swerves away from it.

﴿So whatever you have been given of a thing is an enjoyment of the life of this world﴾. When He (glory be to Him) mentioned the proofs of oneness, He mentioned the warning against this world, meaning: whatever you have been given of wealth and abundance in provision is only a little enjoyment for a few days, which passes and goes away.

Then He encouraged them toward the reward of the Hereafter and what is with God of lasting bliss, and He said: ﴿And what is with God is better and more lasting﴾, meaning: what is with God of reward for acts of obedience and recompense for them with the gardens is better than the enjoyment of this world and more lasting, because it is everlasting and does not end, while the enjoyment of this world ends quickly.

Then He (glory be to Him) explained for whom this is, and He said: ﴿For those who believe﴾, meaning: who are truthful and act according to what faith requires, ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾, meaning: they entrust their affairs to Him and depend upon Him in all their matters, not upon other than Him.

﴿And those who avoid the major sins and the immoralities﴾. The relative pronoun is in the genitive position, coordinated with "those who believe," or a substitute for it, or in the accusative position with an implied "I mean"; the first is preferable. The meaning is: what is with God is better and more lasting for those who believe and for those who avoid.

What is meant by ﴿the major sins of sin﴾ is the major sins among the sins, and we have already established their verification in Surat al-Nisa'.

The majority read "kabā'ir" in the plural, and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "kabīr" in the singular, and it conveys the meaning of the plural, because the genitive construction is generic, like the definite article.

The "fawāḥish" (immoralities) are among the major sins, but with the description of being an immorality they are as if above them, such as murder and fornication and the like. Muqatil said: the immoralities are the causes of the prescribed punishments (mūjibāt al-ḥudūd).

Al-Suddi said: they are fornication.

﴿And when they become angry, they forgive﴾, meaning: they overlook the sin that angered them, restrain their rage, and bear with those who wronged them. Anger was singled out for forgiveness because its dominance over human nature and its overpowering of him is severe, so no one forgives at the surge of anger except one whom God has expanded his chest for and specially favored with the quality of forbearance. For this reason God (glory be to Him) praised them in Al 'Imran by His saying: ﴿And those who restrain their anger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134].

Ibn Zayd said: God made the believers of two kinds: a kind who pardon their wrongdoers, and He began with mentioning them, and a kind who take vengeance on their wrongdoers, and they are those whose mention will come.

﴿And those who respond to their Lord and establish the prayer﴾, meaning: they answered Him in what He called them to, and they upheld what He made obligatory upon them of the obligatory prayer.

Ibn Zayd said: They are the Ansar in Medina, who responded to faith in the Messenger when he sent to them twelve chiefs (naqībs) from among them before the Hijrah, and they established the prayer at its appointed times with its conditions and its forms.

﴿And their affair is by consultation among them﴾, meaning: they consult one another and do not hasten nor act alone in opinion. The word "shūrā" is a verbal noun from "shāwartuhu," like "bushrā" and "dhikrā."

al-Dahhak said: It is their consultation when they heard of the emergence of the Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family and grant him peace) and the arrival of the chiefs to them, when their opinion gathered in the house of Abu Ayyub upon faith in him and support for him.

It was said: what is meant is their consulting in every matter that presents itself to them, so none of them singles out an opinion over the others. How excellent is what Bashshar ibn Burd said:

When opinion reaches the point where consultation is needed, seek help
from the opinion of a sincere advisor or the counsel of a prudent man.
And do not make consultation a burden upon you, for the wing-feathers of a bird are the strength of its primary flight feathers.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 42, verse 29–43 (part 2 of 2):

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to consult his companions in his affairs, and Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to do so, saying: ﴿And consult them in the matter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. We have already discussed consultation (shura) in the commentary on Al 'Imran.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾, i.e., they spend it in the way of good and give charity from it to the needy.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the group that seeks to defend itself against one who wronged it, saying: ﴿And those who, when an oppression afflicts them, they defend themselves﴾. That is, when the oppression of one who oppresses them without right afflicts them. He, glorified is He, mentioned these defenders in the context of praise, just as He mentioned forgiveness at the time of anger in the context of praise, because humbling oneself before the oppressor is not among the attributes of one to whom Allah has given honour, as He said: ﴿And to Allah belongs honour, and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [Al-Munafiqun: 8]. So defending oneself when oppressed is a virtue, just as pardoning at the time of anger is a virtue.

Al-Nakha'i said: "They used to dislike to humiliate themselves, lest the foolish become bold against them."

However, this self-defence is conditional upon confining oneself to what Allah has permitted to him and not exceeding it, as He, glorified is He, explained right after this with His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. So He, glorified is He, made clear that justice in self-defence is to be limited to equivalence. The apparent meaning of this is generality.

Muqatil, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and Sufyan said: this is specific to the one who has been wounded, who may take retaliation from the wounder by way of qisas (retribution), and not otherwise.

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: it is the response to the abusive person when he says, "May Allah disgrace you," so he says, "May Allah disgrace you," without transgressing. Calling the recompense an "evil" is either because it harms the one upon whom it falls, or by way of mushakalah (correspondence in wording), due to the similarity of the two in form.

Then, when He, glorified is He, made clear that the recompense of an evil by its like is a permissible right, He explained the virtue of pardon, saying: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah﴾. That is, whoever pardons one who wronged him and makes reconciliation through the pardon between himself and his oppressor, i.e., Allah, glorified is He, will reward him for that. The reward is left indefinite to magnify its importance and to draw attention to its greatness.

Muqatil said: "So pardon is among the righteous deeds." We have already explained this in the surah of Al 'Imran.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the wrongdoers' departure from His love, which is the cause of success and salvation, saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who initiate wrongdoing. Muqatil said: "He means whoever begins with wrongdoing," and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said the same. It was also said: He does not love whoever exceeds the limit in retaliation and goes beyond the bound in it, because going beyond is wrongdoing.

﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾: this is a verbal noun (masdar) added to its object, i.e., after the wrongdoer had wronged him. The lam is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is the lam of oath, but the first is preferable. The "man" (مَن) is conditional, and its answer is: ﴿those — there is no route (sabil) against them﴾, i.e., no blame or punishment. It is also permissible that "man" be a relative pronoun (al-mawsulah), and the fa' has entered its answer, making the relative pronoun resemble the conditional; but the first is preferable.

When He, glorified is He, negated the route against whoever (p-1332) defends himself after being wronged, He made clear upon whom the route falls, saying: 42 ﴿The route is only against those who wrong people﴾, i.e., who transgress against them initially. So said most of the scholars.

Ibn Jurayj said: i.e., they wrong them by associating partners with Allah, which opposes their religion. ﴿And they commit injustice on the earth without right﴾, i.e., they act against lives and property without right. So said most of the scholars.

Muqatil said: their transgression is their doing of acts of disobedience. It was also said: they act arrogantly and tyrannically.

Abu Malik said: it is what the people of Mecca hoped, that a religion other than Islam would prevail in Mecca. The indication by His saying "those" (أُولَئِكَ) refers to "those who wrong people," and it is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is: ﴿for them is a painful punishment﴾, i.e., for them, by this cause, is a punishment of severe pain.

Then He, glorified is He, encouraged patience and pardon, saying: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives﴾, i.e., is patient over harm and forgives the one who wronged him and does not retaliate. The discussion of this lam and "man" is like the discussion of ﴿and whoever defends himself﴾, that indeed such patience and forgiveness are ﴿of the determined matters (min 'azm al-umur)﴾, i.e., that this is from it, and it was elided for its clarity, as in their saying: "Ghee is two manwas for a dirham."

Muqatil said: "among the matters which Allah has commanded." Al-Zajjaj said: "The patient one is given his patience as a reward, so desire for the reward is more complete in determination." Ibn Zayd said: all of this is abrogated (mansukh) by jihad, and that it is specific to the polytheists.

Qatadah said: it is general, and this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'anic composition. ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾, i.e., for him there is no one after Him who guides him or helps him. The apparent meaning of the verse is generality. It was also said: it is specific to whoever turned away from the Prophet (ﷺ) and did not act upon what he called him to of faith in Allah and acting upon what He legislated. The first is preferable.

Ahmad, Ibn Rahawayh, Ibn Mani', 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim have narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "Shall I inform you of the best verse in the Book of Allah, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related to us: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you, it is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾. I will explain it to you, O 'Ali: whatever affliction, illness, punishment or trial in this world befalls you is because of what your hands have earned; and Allah is too Generous to repeat the punishment upon you in the Hereafter, and what Allah has pardoned in this world, Allah is too Generous to return to it after His pardon."

'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No servant is struck by a calamity, whether great or small, except because of a sin, and what Allah pardons is more numerous." And he recited: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you﴾, the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Kaffarat, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from 'Imran ibn Husayn that some of his companions entered upon him while he had been afflicted in his body, and said: "We are truly distressed for you because of what we see in you." He said: "Do not be distressed by what you see, for what you see is due to a sin, and what Allah pardons is more numerous." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you﴾ to its end.

Ahmad narrated from Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Nothing afflicts the believer in his body, harming him, except that Allah expiates his sins by it."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Bara' who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A slip of the foot, a twitch of a vein, or a scratch of a stick is only because of what your hands have sent forth, and what Allah pardons is more."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿so they remain still upon its back﴾, he said: "They move but do not run in the sea."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿still (rawakid)﴾, he said: "Standing still, or He destroys them," meaning He destroys them.

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'ishah, who said: Zaynab entered upon me while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was with me, and she turned toward me and abused me. The Prophet (ﷺ) restrained her, but she did not stop, so he said to me: "Abuse her." So I abused her until her saliva dried in her mouth, and the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brightened with joy.

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Of two people who revile each other, whatever they say falls upon the one who initiated it, unless the wronged one exceeds the limit." Then he recited: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will command a herald to call out: 'Let whoever has a reward upon Allah stand up.' None will stand except those who pardoned in the world, and that is His saying: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah﴾."

al-Bayhaqi narrated from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "A caller will call out: 'Whoever has a reward upon Allah, let him enter Paradise,' twice, and whoever pardoned his brother will stand up. Allah said: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah﴾."

He (glory be to Him) mentioned some of His signs that demonstrate the perfection of His power, which necessitates His oneness and the truth of what He promised concerning resurrection. He said: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning, their creation in this wondrous manner and with this strange craftsmanship. ﴿And the living creatures He has dispersed in both﴾ may be connected to "creation," and it may be connected to "the heavens." The "dābba" (living creature) is the name for everything that crawls.

Al-Farra' said: He meant what He dispersed in the earth without the heaven, as in His saying: ﴿From them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], and they only emerge from the salt water and not from the sweet.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: Its estimated meaning is "and what He dispersed in one of the two," so the genitive noun was omitted.

Mujahid said: This includes the angels and the humans, and God Most High has said: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾ [al-Naml: 8]. ﴿And He is, when He wills, over their gathering﴾, meaning, their assembling (ḥashr) on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿competent﴾. The temporal clause is connected to "their gathering," not to "competent." Abu al-Baqa' said: because otherwise it would result in: "He is competent over their gathering when He wills," so that power would be linked to will, and that is impossible.

Shihab al-Din said: I do not know what makes it impossible according to the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah. If he is speaking according to the view of the Mu'tazilah, namely that power relates to what God did not will, then his statement stands, but that is a corrupt doctrine that is not permissible to hold.

﴿And whatever affliction befalls you, it is for what your hands have earned﴾, meaning: whatever afflictions befall you, whatever they may be, it is because of what your hands have earned of sins.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "bimā kasabat" without the fa', and the rest read it with the fa'. The "mā" in ﴿wa-mā aṣābakum﴾ is conditional (shartiyyah), and for this reason the fa' entered its response according to the reading of the majority. Its omission is not permissible according to Sibawayh and the majority. Al-Akhfash permitted the omission, as in His saying: ﴿And if you obey them, you are indeed polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 121], and in the words of the poet:

Whoever does good deeds, God will reward them,
and evil with evil, with God, is like for like.

It was also said that it is the relative (mawsulah) "mā," and then both omission and inclusion would be permissible, but the first is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: Including the fa' is better, because the fa' is the apodosis (mujāzāt jawāb al-shart) of the conditional. Whoever omits the fa' does so on the basis that "mā" means "alladhī" (that which), and the meaning is: "That which afflicted you occurred because of what your hands have earned."

Al-Hasan said: The affliction here refers to the prescribed punishments (ḥudūd) for sins. But the preferable view is to take it in its generality, as indicated by the indefinite noun occurring in a negative context and the inclusion of "min" (of) as expressing totality on it. ﴿And He pardons much﴾ of the sins which the servants commit, so He does not punish for them. The meaning of the verse is that He expiates for the servant by means of the afflictions that befall him, and pardons much of the sins.

Sound evidences have established that everything a person is afflicted with in this world is either rewarded for him or expiated from his sins.

It was also said that this verse is specific to the disbelievers, in the sense that what they are afflicted with is because of their sins, without that being an expiation for a sin or an acquisition of reward, and that their punishment is left aside for much of their sins, so He does not hasten to punish them in this world but gives them respite until the Last Abode.

The preferable view is to take the verse in its generality, and pardon (ʿafw) applies both to the postponement of punishment and to the erasure of the sin and the lifting of address (khiṭāb) concerning it.

Al-Wahidi said: This is the most hopeful (arjā) verse in the Book of God, because He made the sins of the believers of two kinds: one kind He expiates from them through afflictions, and another kind He pardons in this world, and He is Generous and does not retract His pardon. This is the custom of God with the believers.

As for the disbeliever, his sin is not hastened in punishment for him until he is brought to account for it on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And you cannot escape in the earth﴾, meaning: you cannot flee from it by fleeing in the earth or in the heaven, even if you were in them; rather, what He has decreed upon them of afflictions befalls them and descends upon them. ﴿And you have no protector other than God﴾ who would support you and thereby avert what God has decreed, ﴿nor any helper who would help you against the punishment of God, in this world or in the Hereafter.﴾

Then He (glory be to Him) mentioned another of His great signs, which demonstrate His oneness and the truth of what He promised, and He said: ﴿And among His signs are the ships﴾. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "al-jawārī" with the "yā'" affirmed when connected; when stopping, its affirmation is according to the original form and its omission is for lightening. They are the ships, the singular of which is "jāriyah," meaning "sailing," ﴿on the sea like mountains﴾, meaning like the mountains, the plural of "'alam," which is a mountain. From it is the saying of al-Khansa':

Indeed Sakhr, the guided ones take him as a guide,
as if he were a beacon with fire on its summit.

Al-Khalil said: Everything elevated among the Arabs is an "'alam." Mujahid said: "al-a'lām" are palaces, whose singular is "'alam."

﴿If He wills, He calms the wind﴾. The majority read "yashā'" with a hamzah, and Warsh from Nafi' read it without a hamzah. The majority read "al-rīḥ" in the singular, and Nafi' read "al-riyāḥ" in the plural, meaning: He calms the wind by which the ships sail, ﴿so they remain motionless (fa-yaẓlalna)﴾, meaning, the ships become stationary, still, fixed, ﴿upon its back﴾, the back of the sea.

It is said: "rakada al-mā'u rukūdan" meaning the water became still; likewise "rakadat al-rīḥ" and "rakadat al-safīnah," and everything fixed in a place is "rākid."

The majority read "fa-yaẓlalna" with the first lām pronounced with a fatha, and Qatadah read it with a kasra, which is a rare dialect.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, that which has been mentioned of the matter of the ships, there are signs, great proofs, ﴿for every steadfast, grateful person﴾, meaning, for everyone who is greatly patient in trials and greatly thankful for blessings.

Qutrub said: "al-Ṣabbār" is the one who is very grateful, who when he is given, gives thanks, and when he is tested, is patient.

'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah said:

How many a person blessed who is not grateful,
and how many a person tested who is not patient.

﴿Or He destroys them for what they have earned﴾: it is coordinated with "yuskin" (He calms), meaning He destroys them by drowning, and what is meant is that He destroys them for what they have earned of sins.

It was also said: for what they associated (with Him).

The first is preferable, for He destroys in the sea both the polytheist and the non-polytheist. It is said: "awbaqahu," meaning he destroyed him. ﴿And He pardons much﴾ of its people by overlooking their sins, so He saves them from drowning.

The majority read "yaʿfu" in the jussive, coordinated with the response of the conditional. Al-Qushayri said: There is a problem with this reading, because the meaning would be: "If He wills, He calms the wind, so those ships remain stationary, or He destroys them for the sins of their people." It is not good to coordinate "yaʿfu" with this, because the meaning would become: "If He wills, He pardons," and that is not the meaning. Rather the meaning is the report of pardon without a condition of will. So it is coordinated with the jussive in form, not in meaning. Some read "wa-yaʿfū" with the nominative, and it is good in meaning.

Abu Hayyan said: What he said is not good, since the meaning of the construction is not understood. The meaning is: only that He, Most High, destroyed some people and saved others by way of pardoning them. Al-A'mash read "wa-yaʿfū" with the nominative. Some people of Medina read it in the accusative, with "an" implied after the "wa," as in the saying of al-Nabighah:

If Abu Qabus perishes, the spring of the people will perish, and the sacred month,
and we will take after him by the tails of a life, a back thin of hump, without a hump.

With the accusative of "wa-na'khudha."

﴿And that those who dispute concerning Our signs may know that they have no escape﴾. The majority read "yaʿlam" in the accusative. Al-Zajjaj said: "ʿalā al-ṣarf." He said: The meaning of "ṣarf" is turning the coordination from the wording to the coordination with the meaning. He said: Because it was not good to coordinate "wa-yaʿlam" as jussive with what precedes it, since the meaning would be "if He wills with knowledge," he turned to coordinating it with the verbal noun (maṣdar) of the verb that precedes it, and that is only possible by implying "an," so that it with the verb becomes in the sense of a noun. And from this are the two verses of al-Nabighah mentioned shortly before. As al-Zajjaj said, al-Mubarrad and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said that, but this view has been objected to with things of no value.

It was also said: the accusative is by coordination on a deleted causal clause, and the estimated meaning is: "so that He may take vengeance on them and know."

Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that what follows from the condition is the destruction of some people and the salvation of others, so it is not good to estimate "so that He may take vengeance on them."

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "yaʿlamu" in the nominative, as a resumptive (isti'nāf) clause. This reading is clear in meaning and plain in wording.

It was also read in the jussive, coordinated with the preceding jussive, meaning: "And if He wills, He combines between destruction, salvation, and warning."

The meaning of ﴿they have no escape﴾ is that they have no flight and no refuge, as said by Qutrub.

al-Suddi said: They have no refuge, and it is derived from the saying of the people: "ḥāṣa bihi al-baʿīr ḥaysatan," when the camel threw him off, and from it the saying: "Fulan yaḥīṣu ʿan al-ḥaqq," meaning he swerves away from it.

﴿So whatever you have been given of a thing is an enjoyment of the life of this world﴾. When He (glory be to Him) mentioned the proofs of oneness, He mentioned the warning against this world, meaning: whatever you have been given of wealth and abundance in provision is only a little enjoyment for a few days, which passes and goes away.

Then He encouraged them toward the reward of the Hereafter and what is with God of lasting bliss, and He said: ﴿And what is with God is better and more lasting﴾, meaning: what is with God of reward for acts of obedience and recompense for them with the gardens is better than the enjoyment of this world and more lasting, because it is everlasting and does not end, while the enjoyment of this world ends quickly.

Then He (glory be to Him) explained for whom this is, and He said: ﴿For those who believe﴾, meaning: who are truthful and act according to what faith requires, ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾, meaning: they entrust their affairs to Him and depend upon Him in all their matters, not upon other than Him.

﴿And those who avoid the major sins and the immoralities﴾. The relative pronoun is in the genitive position, coordinated with "those who believe," or a substitute for it, or in the accusative position with an implied "I mean"; the first is preferable. The meaning is: what is with God is better and more lasting for those who believe and for those who avoid.

What is meant by ﴿the major sins of sin﴾ is the major sins among the sins, and we have already established their verification in Surat al-Nisa'.

The majority read "kabā'ir" in the plural, and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "kabīr" in the singular, and it conveys the meaning of the plural, because the genitive construction is generic, like the definite article.

The "fawāḥish" (immoralities) are among the major sins, but with the description of being an immorality they are as if above them, such as murder and fornication and the like. Muqatil said: the immoralities are the causes of the prescribed punishments (mūjibāt al-ḥudūd).

Al-Suddi said: they are fornication.

﴿And when they become angry, they forgive﴾, meaning: they overlook the sin that angered them, restrain their rage, and bear with those who wronged them. Anger was singled out for forgiveness because its dominance over human nature and its overpowering of him is severe, so no one forgives at the surge of anger except one whom God has expanded his chest for and specially favored with the quality of forbearance. For this reason God (glory be to Him) praised them in Al 'Imran by His saying: ﴿And those who restrain their anger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134].

Ibn Zayd said: God made the believers of two kinds: a kind who pardon their wrongdoers, and He began with mentioning them, and a kind who take vengeance on their wrongdoers, and they are those whose mention will come.

﴿And those who respond to their Lord and establish the prayer﴾, meaning: they answered Him in what He called them to, and they upheld what He made obligatory upon them of the obligatory prayer.

Ibn Zayd said: They are the Ansar in Medina, who responded to faith in the Messenger when he sent to them twelve chiefs (naqībs) from among them before the Hijrah, and they established the prayer at its appointed times with its conditions and its forms.

﴿And their affair is by consultation among them﴾, meaning: they consult one another and do not hasten nor act alone in opinion. The word "shūrā" is a verbal noun from "shāwartuhu," like "bushrā" and "dhikrā."

al-Dahhak said: It is their consultation when they heard of the emergence of the Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family and grant him peace) and the arrival of the chiefs to them, when their opinion gathered in the house of Abu Ayyub upon faith in him and support for him.

It was said: what is meant is their consulting in every matter that presents itself to them, so none of them singles out an opinion over the others. How excellent is what Bashshar ibn Burd said:

When opinion reaches the point where consultation is needed, seek help
from the opinion of a sincere advisor or the counsel of a prudent man.
And do not make consultation a burden upon you, for the wing-feathers of a bird are the strength of its primary flight feathers.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 42, verse 29–43 (part 2 of 2):

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to consult his companions in his affairs, and Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to do so, saying: ﴿And consult them in the matter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. We have already discussed consultation (shura) in the commentary on Al 'Imran.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾, i.e., they spend it in the way of good and give charity from it to the needy.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the group that seeks to defend itself against one who wronged it, saying: ﴿And those who, when an oppression afflicts them, they defend themselves﴾. That is, when the oppression of one who oppresses them without right afflicts them. He, glorified is He, mentioned these defenders in the context of praise, just as He mentioned forgiveness at the time of anger in the context of praise, because humbling oneself before the oppressor is not among the attributes of one to whom Allah has given honour, as He said: ﴿And to Allah belongs honour, and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [Al-Munafiqun: 8]. So defending oneself when oppressed is a virtue, just as pardoning at the time of anger is a virtue.

Al-Nakha'i said: "They used to dislike to humiliate themselves, lest the foolish become bold against them."

However, this self-defence is conditional upon confining oneself to what Allah has permitted to him and not exceeding it, as He, glorified is He, explained right after this with His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. So He, glorified is He, made clear that justice in self-defence is to be limited to equivalence. The apparent meaning of this is generality.

Muqatil, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and Sufyan said: this is specific to the one who has been wounded, who may take retaliation from the wounder by way of qisas (retribution), and not otherwise.

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: it is the response to the abusive person when he says, "May Allah disgrace you," so he says, "May Allah disgrace you," without transgressing. Calling the recompense an "evil" is either because it harms the one upon whom it falls, or by way of mushakalah (correspondence in wording), due to the similarity of the two in form.

Then, when He, glorified is He, made clear that the recompense of an evil by its like is a permissible right, He explained the virtue of pardon, saying: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah﴾.
